speechtext: On the orders of the day:

In answer to the question asked by the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I table a document showing the permanent appointments to revenue postmasterships made between August 7, 1930, and February 28, 1935, by provinces and electoral districts; also a document showing the temporary appointments to revenue postmasterships during the same period. The compilation of the list of these appointments required the perusal of more than 4,300 records and more than 1,000 supplementary hours of work, 360 of which were outside the regular hours, at night, on Saturday afternoon and Sunday. To answer as quickly as possible we had to suspend in part the regular work and to get it up to date, will require extra hours of work.
I thank the minister and I am delighted to see that at last he has waked up.
On the orders of the day:

Yesterday the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) inquired regarding the proposal of the government in respect of the adjournment of the house over Easter. The Prime Minister is making steady progress towards recovery. Yesterday he sat up for a time and I saw him afterwards and he looked exceedingly well. We all expect that he will be well enough to attend the ceremonies of the King's Jubilee in London on May 6. I am sure that everyone in this house and in the country would like to see Canada represented by the Prime Minister on that historic occasion. It is our intention to ask this house to consent to an adjournment until Monday, the 20th day of May, by which time-

Oh!

Easter Adjournment

I quite realize that some hon. gentlemen would prefer to have the adjournment not so long, but under the circumstances I hope they will acquiesce, because by that time we expect the Prime Minister to be back in Canada and able to take up his duties again in this house. We certainly think it is very desirable that the Prime Minister should be here when parliament is prorogued. In the meantime it is our intention to get legislation prepared, based on the mass buying commission's report, which the chairman tells me is expected to be ready for presentation to the Minister of Trade and Commerce next Tuesday, and which we hope to be able to lay on the table of the house some day next week. There is also legislation which will be based on the report which it is hoped the housing committee will make next week too. Our purpose is to have that legislation prepared during the recess, so that when we come back we will be able to complete the session as quickly as possible, and I am sure every hon, member will like to see that done.
By the middle of July.

No; I am sure the legislation that will be introduced will be so satisfactory to the hon. gentleman that he will find himself unable to oppose it, in exactly the same way as he has found himself unable to oppose the legislation which has been brought in this session already.
There was nothing to oppose.

We propose to submit to the house an estimate for the payment of the actual moving or transportation expenses and reasonable living expenses of the members in the same way as was done during the recess at the end of 1932. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) proposes to include that in his supplementary estimates.
Will it include the payment of rents for apartments?

I am sorry to say that we cannot cover every case, and we propose to deal with the matter as has been done in other similar years.
With regard to the time when parliament will be able to adjourn for the Easter recess, I am unable to give my hon. friends opposite any better information than they have themselves in what was said yesterday. If we are to have this adjournment until May 20, we can adjourn at the convenience of hon. members on any day when business warrants.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
It is unnecessary to say that we are greatly pleased to learn that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is making such a good recovery. I also think the house will be pleased to know the Prime Minister hopes to find it possible to be present at the silver jubilee ceremonies in London. The country will wish to be represented there at that time by him. But I am sorry to hear my right hon. friend say that he thinks it will be necessary to have such a long adjournment at the Easter season. May I say to the acting leader of the government that I think he has got along splendidly; we all seem to be managing very well with his colleagues and himself and we have got through a great deal of business. I see no reason why that happy condition of affairs should not continue with the acting leader in charge and without any loss to the Prime Minister or to the country. While it is of course most important that we should have the report of the price spreads commission and the legislation that is to be based thereon, and in addition the report of the housing committee, still I believe a recess of something like a week or ten days at Easter would be ample, and we might get under way with that legislation before the return of the Prime Minister from the conference in time to permit him to close the session as he will no doubt very much wish to do. But I feel a very strong protest ought to be made against adjourning for so long a time as until May 20, and tihat notwithstanding the compensation which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) is going to give us all for expenses in going to and from our residences at that time.
The really serious part of the whole matter is that this unnecessary prolongation of the work of the session means a still further postponement of the date of the general election. There is no doubt in the world that until after there has been a general election, business will not begin to become normal, or a general revival take place. For that reason I wish to protest again at so long a delay at the Easter season.

I thought my right hon. friend might to some extent criticise the length of the adjournment; but might I say, when he suggests it would further postpone the date of the general election, he is entirely in error. The revision of the lists is now under way, and as soon as those lists are completed, we shall be able to have an election. Whether we sit in May or June will make no difference in the date.

Easter Adjournment
Can the right hon. gentleman say when we may expect to have the lists completed?
The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) will reply to that.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speechtext: That will depend upon the number of alterations which are made in the lists as now printed and published. I cannot express an opinion as to the time it will take to make those corrections in the presently existing lists.
Has my hon. friend any idea as to how many changes will have to be made, and would it be possible for him to make an estimate in the next few days?

I have no knowledge of constituencies other than my own, but I am informed, whether reliably or not, that in the lists of 25,000 or 26,000 voters in that district, there may be at least 2,500 or 3,000 changes. In some years I have known of more than that number to take place on or about May 1.

While we might well feel it regrettable that there must be such a long adjournment, under the circumstances I presume it will be necessary for us to acquiesce in the government's request; but if during that long adjournment, the government is able to prepare some worthwhile legislation, probably the adjournment may also be worth while.
There is however one point that I would like to impress upon the present leader of the house (Sir George Perley), and that is that seeing the adjournment must be of some considerable length, it would be advisable to let hon. members know as early as possible on what date the adjournment will take place in order that we may make our plans.

May I ask the acting leader of the government whether any new legislation will be introduced between now and the time of the adjournment, and also whether when the house reassembles after adjournment, the legislation that will then be introduced will be limited to what is based on the report of the price spreads commission and the report of the housing committee in addition to what we already have on the order paper?

As regards
legislation that may be introduced between now and the date of adjournment, there may be one or two other bills; we will let the right hon. gentleman know as early as possible.

As to legislation that may be brought in after the adjournment, all I can promise is that we shall try to have it all ready within a day or two after we meet.

I would like to have
the indulgence of the house to make a few remarks on the administration of the mounted police. The other day when certain estimates were up hon. members complained of the manner in which some of the officials were carrying on their work. About a month ago there was brought to my knowledge by one of the most prominent barristers and solicitors of our city the fact that one evening he was in his office a little after 6.30-

speechtext: Order.

His wife called him and advised him that some officers of the mounted police were at their house saying that they were to carry out an investigation. Of course he said to his wife that there was no objection, to let them go on. They proceeded to go over the house from top to bottom to find out whether there was
liquor concealed anywhere on the premises. I do not wish to give in this house the name of the barrister who told me of this incident because I did not tell him I would bring the case to the attention of the house. This gentleman and his wife and his family were put to serious annoyance and disturbance, and I repeat that this man is one of the leading members of the bar in the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal. Of course the mounted police did not find anything, and they went out saying they were sorry. A few days afterwards I had occasion to meet one of the solicitors of the government who were handling some of those cases in Montreal, and I reported the facts to him. He said, Well, we have no control over those things. It might happen that certain residences on given streets would be assigned to certain officers of the mounted police to investigate. I asked that friend of mine, Did they show any document or warrant or authority for going there? He said, No, they just presented themselves in the evening and said they were men of the mounted police and had the right to look through the house. As I could not get any satisfactory answer from the lawyers representing the government I thought it my duty to bring this case to the attention of the committee in order that the Minister of Justice and officials of the mounted police might find out whether it is the practice to give blanket instructions and certain street numbers to their officers to which they can go at random, and maybe one day go to some high official or persons higher in society than this prominent lawyer, who might be disturbed at any hour of the evening or night. I strongly protest against this practice and hope such an incident will not be repeated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will write me a letter and give me some particulars I shall have inquiry made. If it is only a general charge without particulars I do not know that I can assist him. He need not disclose names, but if he will give me date and place probably I can get reports. I may tell him that no blanket instructions are given as to certain streets or blocks; such blanket instructions do not exist. When information comes that illicit traffic in liquor is being carried on, then under what is known as a writ of assistance issued under the Customs and Excise Acts, the mounted police under the provisions of that act are entitled to make search. But the instructions are very specific, no general instructions are

issued. If my hon. friend will tell me in confidence the place and date I will have a report made and presented to him.

Some time ago I had occasion to write to the minister asking him a question, and I am obliged to say that I have received no answer. Here is the case. Some time ago a man was accused of having liquor in his possession, contrary to the Excise Act. He was tried and acquitted. A couple of days afterwards the mounted police went to his place, his wife and children being there, and asked him for his finger prints. The man refused. The mounted police forced him to give his finger prints. He had been acquitted of the charge. I do not see how the mounted police could have authority to go there and force him to give his finger prints. This man wrote a letter to me enclosing a letter for the Minister of Justice, and I wrote the minister myself asking what authority the police officers had to take finger prints under such circumstances. I have received no answer and would ask the minister to give me an answer now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I may tell my hon.
friend that a report was received by me at five minutes to three this afternoon on the case he mentions. He will be notified by letter to-morrow as to the contents of the report. I only glanced over it before coming into the house, not knowing this question was coming up. But I may tell him that when any indictable offence is charged it is permissible under the law to take finger prints.
Is it permissible after he is acquitted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot speak as to that. My information at the moment is that they can take finger prints at any time when a man is charged with an indictable offence. I shall have to look into it and make a more detailed report to my hon. friend. But after glancing at the report my recollection is that his acquittal was appealed.
The case is in appeal now. I understand that he was acquitted and then the government appealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then he may still be convicted; I thought I gathered that from the report, but I will write my hon. friend to-morrow. I do not think there has been any delay in this matter; I think I have
(Mr. Guthrie.]
the reputation of answering my correspondence pretty promptly. I know some criticism is levelled against some of the departments, but I do not think that applies to my department.

I quite endorse what has been said by the minister, that there is no delay on his part in dealing with cases that come before him, and also, perhaps inferentially, that any case with which he may have to deal is considered fairly and with every consideration shown the accused. But I say to this committee that regardless of what may happen in any case, large or small, that may come before any of the courts of this country, to take the finger prints of any man accused simply because he has been accused, before the final disposition of his case has been made, is an outrage and ought to be condemned by every member of this house. I have no hesitation in saying that so far as I am concerned it will receive all the opposition that is within my power.

I offer my congratulations to my hon. friend from West Hamilton for the statement he has just made, which is worthy of his experience before the courts, especially in criminal matters. May I ask the minister what have been the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in fighting communism in this country? I should like to know something about the stand taken by officer Zaneth in the prosecution of communists in Toronto some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Officer Zaneth had nothing to do with the matter; he was never connected in any way with prosecutions in Toronto.
But were there any prosecutions of communists after the report was secured by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The attorney general of
Ontario took action and he asked for reports from the mounted police. The action was entirely in the hands of the attorney general's department in Toronto.

I remember that at the
time I received a communication about it from Mr. Price, then attorney general, which I believe was sent to all hon. members. Then may I ask the minister this very direct question: Are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police doing anything to secure information about the communists or to check communist propaganda in this country?

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, no special effort is
being made in regard to communism, but they do take general cognizance of what is going on throughout Canada, and if anything unusual happens they report it. I do not know of any action ever having been taken by the mounted police in regard to that matter.

May I ask the hon.
gentleman if some booklets containing communistic propaganda were seized by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My instructions are in
the negative.

Is there not someone in
the mounted police who checks the papers published in foreign languages in order to bring to the attention of the commissioner anything by way of communistic propaganda?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh yes, I think probably the foreign newspapers as well as newspapers that are not in foreign languages, are checked up.

And may I ask the minister if there is not a translator in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police branch whose business it is to read publications in foreign
languages with regard to the communistic propaganda in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, not particularly in
regard to communists, but in regard to all foreign newspapers and particularly those that are under suspicion of publishing matter detrimental to Canada or to the government of Canada or anything of the kind. We have had intimations from foreign powers in regard to some foreign language publications in Canada reflecting on Jugoslavia and other countries, threatening the destruction of the king and the like, and we have translators or we get translations done by some departs ment of the government; I think probably the mounted police are able to make the translations themselves. I have had protests from representatives of foreign states, consuls and the like, and we are in a position to translate and scrutinize the contents of foreign language newspapers.

Then would the minister
be kind enough to tell the committee in what sense they are scrutinized and for what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For general purposes.
This work is very confidential; it is part of the secret service work of the mounted police.

I am very glad indeed to hear the statement of the minister; it is in accord with a speech delivered by the Prime Minister in Toronto as reported in the Ottawa Evening Citizen of Thursday, November 10, 1932. The title is:
Asks Canadians Put Iron Heel on Communism
Premier Bennett also vigorously denounces socialism in address to Ontario Conservative Association. Says Liberals seem to capitalize on unrest. Declares cooperative commonwealth movement means sovietism.
The article continues:
Toronto, November 9.-In a vigorous speech which carried applause from every corner of the convention hall, Prime Minister, R. B. Bennett, to-day roundly denounced socialism and communism. Premier Bennett was addressing the 11th annual convention of the Ontario Conservative Association.
What do these so-called groups of socialists and communists offer you? the Prime Minister asked. "Some are commending to you the history of Russia," Mr. Bennett declared. "If any of you have read the small volume by the Duchess of Athol], I do not think you will give it much support."
Then he continues as follows:
"They are sowing their seeds everywhere. Right in this city of Toronto such propaganda is being carried on, and in the little out of the way places the same injurious work is being done. We know that throughout Canada this propaganda is being put forward by organizations from foreign lands that seek to destroy our institutions. Now, ladies and gentlemen, we ask every true Canadian to put the iron heel of ruthlessness against a thing of that kind."
This was the address by the Prime Minister, and I understand that the only time a heel is used as a rudder is when the toboggan is going down the hill. He continued:
Well, if there are any Liberals within sound of my voice you will get away from that party because it is no longer a party but a jumble led by a cooperative commonwealth. Why? Because they seek to capitalize on all the unrest that exists.
The Prime Minister closed with a cheerful note of optimism. Canadians would go through the economic situation successfully, and was maintaining its stand' as the fifth trading nation of the world.
Then if we glance at the New York Times of February 17, 1935, we see this heading: Bolshevism Marches Toward Its Goal
An examination reveals that Russia has carried out the major Marxist principles.
Therefore as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is securing information about the dangers of communist propaganda it is safeguarding the old order of things. Old order or no order, this is a most important thing, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a bulwark of the old order. But unfortunately,

as the Prime Minister has said, the old order has gone. Therefore the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is fighting for an aim which is in contradiction of the aim held by the Prime Minister. The right hon. gentleman has said the old order has gone, but we find the Royal Canadian Mounted Police fighting for it. This is a most serious thing. It is so serious that I shall ask that police body to safeguard the country and the order of things against those who preach communistic propaganda in Canada. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police must be very careful, and would render a very great service by protecting the old order against the dangerous innovations of some so-called statesmen.
The Prime Minister.

Therefore I suggest they
should have a guard around the Chateau Laurier so that in the event of the Prime Minister recuperating-and I sincerely hope he will

he will not make any more statements such as the one I shall now read. This statement would have been confiscated by the police had it been uttered by any other Canadian citizen. Mark you, sir, the Times, the greatest paper published on this continent, states:

The first time the Prime Minister spoke about the iron heel of ruthlessness he was influenced by a book published by the Duchess of Athol. This time he is influenced by Strachey, by Criipps and by Litvinoff.

Temiscouata is dealing with the inactivities of the mounted police.

I want the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to do their duty, to be a useful body in this country, and not simply to sit in their offices without performing the duties for which they were appointed, and for which we vote money. That is why I want to give them a very good tip as to a most useful work they can do by indicating to them most dangerous and most pernicious communist propaganda which came out of the lips of the Prime Minister, and I ask the commissioner to stop that communist propaganda in this country. Now I am through, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman,
may I just say a very brief word in regard to what has been advanced to the committee by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat? If I have followed, and I hope I have, the questions that he addressed to the hon. Minister of Justice, they were designed to crystallize, so to speak, the activities of the mounted police in various parts of this country, and particularly in those realms with which the hon. member for Temiscouata is best acquainted. I have followed with great interest tjie balance of his address based on what my hon. friend was able, I will not say to elicit from the minister, but to suggest to the minister, and that brings me to one thought of very grave necessity. In this house last night when the penitentiary estimates were under consideration I felt constrained to offer to the Department of Justice
TMr. Pouliot.)
the suggestion that there should be in every penitentiary in this country a competent psychiatric clinic. Having listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata this afternoon I am constrained to suggest that that might be extended to certain members of parliament, and particularly to the hon. gentleman from Temiscouata.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
attach much importance to what the hon. member from Hamilton (Mr. Bell) has said. I will leave with him this one thought, that people who live in glass houses should be very careful not to throw stones. I was generous enough to offer my congratulations to him at the beginning of this sitting, but now I gladly withdraw them because he is not worthy of them.

I am flattered,
highly flattered.

When the bill regarding the
Royal Canadian Mounted Police was under discussion some time ago I mentioned at that time some matters affecting the force and its operations in the province of British Columbia. The minister, in reply at that time, said that perhaps these matters could be better discussed when the estimates were under consideration. On that occasion I did not go as fully into the matter as I should have liked, nor did I mention the names .of those connected who had been engaged by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. However, I am taking the opportunity this afternoon to bring these matters to the minister's attention, and I take it that he has under his hand all the information regarding these cases.
The first case is that of a man named Handley who was engaged as an under cover man for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He operated from Vancouver throughout the lower Fraser valley, but particularly in the municipality of Richmond, and I may say that he was operating there without the knowledge of the municipal police. Whether any information had been given to the provincial police I do not know, but I do know that he was operating in the various municipalities without any knowledge on the part of the municipal police, either regarding his operations or regarding the workings of the other under cover men. From information I have, and I have been in very close touch with the reeves of the various municipalities, there has been no necessity to call in the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, especially in the cases which I am going to discuss. I have every word of praise both for

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
the provincial and far the municipal police, nor have I anything particularly derogatory to say of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; it is the operations of the under cover men which I wish to discuss particularly this afternoon, while the chief officer of the mounted police is before him.
The first case occurred on March 20, 1934. It was then that this man Handley went into a store operated by a Chinaman and asked him if he would like to make money by selling liquor. After some negotiations the Chinaman consented, and Handley offered to supply him with battles, colouring mater and labels.
I take strong objection, as I did the last time the matter was under discussion, to any man being allowed to go through the municipalities and tempt men to commit crime. I do not think it is the duty or (the business of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to butt in in these municipalities in this class of work. On April 6 the place was searched by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and this man came before the court. The municipal police were not aware that Handley was operating under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but they did have information that he was handling liquor and had liquor in his charge for sale. Not knowing that he was operating under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police they arrested him. It was when they arrested him that the information then came out that he was an under cover man in the employ of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Charges were laid-and I have copies of the court record under my hand. He came before the court and both he and a confederate named Kemp, who sometimes operated under the name of Tufts, were fined $500 or six months. During the time the case was pending the municipal police endeavoured to obtain information regarding this man Handley, and on being tipped off from the Vancouver police department that he had a criminal record and was wanted for a certain crime in Australia they went to the immigration authorities and there endeavoured to get his record. I call the minister's attention to this aspect of the matter, though it does not come directly under his department, because it is very serious. The immigration authorities refused to give any information; they said they had instructions from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police not to divulge information to the municipal or any other police force regarding this man. The municipal police then wired Australia and information -came from that country regarding the man's record. It appears he had come to Canada as a stowaway, landing in Montreal, and had travelled across the
country to Vancouver, entering the country through the port of Vancouver even though he had declared that he was a stowaway. The following day his wife and family arrived from Australia and they also were admitted into the country. That question does not come directly under the jurisdiction of the minister, but I shall probably have more to say regarding it when the immigration estimates are under discussion, because I believe it to be a very serious state of affairs. I corroborated the information regarding the stand taken by the immigration authorities, as when I was asked to come into this matter, an appeal being made to me by the reeve of the municipality and the chief of police, I discussed the case with the immigration authorities, who told me that they knew better than to do anything against the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I made the statement at the time, and I make it now, that it seemed to me, so far as that department was concerned, that all you had to do was to be employed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and you were immune from arrest or deportation no matter what your crime was and thalt any information regarding your record would also be withheld.
I do not know whether the minister has before him the full record of this man, but Handley was at one time in partnership with a man named Springer, running a gas station and a car repair establishment. The police found alcohol on the premises and a charge was laid against Springer, though not against Handley, who was, as I have stated, working for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There was another case where a man named Walker purchased liquor through Handley and this man Walker was convicted. In this connection, I should like to know who received the moieties in these cases, and what amounts were paid. Handley also sold smuggled cigarettes. I mention this in order to show the minister that a man without character, about whom the Royal Canadian Mounted Police presumably knew nothing at first, though they certainly did afterwards, a fugitive from justice from some other country where he was wanted for crime, was let loose throughout the lower Fraser valley where he deliberately went about offering either cigarettes or liquor to anyone he came in contact with, and if people were weak or foolish enough to fall for it, a report was then made to the police and they were picked up. This man offered cigarettes to one Kemp of the Pacific Bottle Company. The cigarettes were seized by the police and the man was convicted. Again, I would ask, who got

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
the moiety in that case? Handley purchased his liquor from a man in Seattle, and it would be interesting to know how he and others were able to cross the line back and forth with bottles, labels, colouring matter and liquor. I can give the names and addresses to show where the supplies were procured across the line. I want to know whether the immigration and customs authorities were aware of this man's identity when he was travelling back and forth. I am told, but I am not sure of it, that they were not. However, he purchased this liquor from a man named Anderson of Seattle, Washington, and he bought the colouring and flavouring from Lyons' drug store there. He even offered to sell narcotics. He was dealing in contraband cigarettes, liquor and dope. He left a tin of alcohol with a man named La Pierre, who lives on the border near Bellingham, and he was asked whether Eddie Tufts had asked him to smuggle cigarettes into British Columbia for him. During the adjournment of the first hearing of the charge under the liquor act, which was in May, 1934, Handley and Kemp went across the line and on their return endeavoured to sell moonshine to a man named J. Ross, who operates a hotel in the town of Mission, British Columbia, but were unsuccessful. At the time of his arrest on May 2, 1934, he had a bottle of moonshine in his possession which he had placed in an oil pit at a gas service station before his arrest. These two men, Handley and Kemp, worked together. I think I am correct in stating that Kemp was not exactly in the pay of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but Handley was: Handley was, I understand, receiving $160 but Tufts or Kemp was receiving moieties for the information laid before the police and they split on the moieties. Kemp's operations were along the same lines as those of Mr. Handley.
Another case not exactly of the same character is that of a man named Sawley. Sawley lived in the city of Vancouver. He was accosted one day and asked if he would like to make some money. Being idle and having been idle for a year and a half he naturally answered, yes. I am not going into all the details of how the contact was made, but to state the matter briefly, Sawley went out to a place a little beyond Abbotsford and there picked up several gallon tins of alcohol. He was successful the first time in reaching Vancouver with it, but on his second trip a week or so later he fell asleep at the wheel during the night for just a minute and his car went into the ditch and overturned. After he regained consciousness and got up, the first 
thing he did was to lift the tins of alcohol and put them up on the bank. His story to the chief of police, to me and to the neighbouring chief of police, repeated on three occasions, was that after he waited there a while, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police came along and seeing him on the roadside in the car, stopped. But the remarks which were made to him, according to his statement, are worthy of note. They said that they had been waiting for Sawley and as he was an hour and a half or more overdue, they thought they would set out and look for him. What [DOT] I want to draw to the attention of the minister is this. H they had information regarding this man Sawley and were lying in wait for him coming from near the boundary line to the city of Vancouver, why did they not make a circle around that ring of men who brought the liquor across the line and transferred it from one car to the other which Sawley was driving rather than simply wait until the one mam came along and pick him up? That aspect of the matter should be looked into, because they seemed to know all about this man Sawley and his operations.
I have many other cases, but I am not going to deal with all of them unless I have to; I have sworn affidavits and information in connection with a whole raft of cases. Somebody suggests that I use the word "declarations." I will call them declarations so that we may not split hairs between a man's affidavit and his declaration.
The next is a radio case which I think is fairly serious; it is to me rather an outstanding case. This -man was afterwards interviewed by one of the provincial police force who went to see him. It appears that some time in February or March, 1934, Herbert Handley came into the store and looked at a small pocket radio which this Mr. Nemetz wanted to get rid of as there was no sale for such a thing. He offered it for $10 to Mr. Handley. Handley mentioned some names as references, took the radio and was to bring his own back in exchange. He came back in a few days with a small radio which he said he would give in exchange for the one he took away and he told the storekeeper Nemetz to try it out. A short time after Mr. Handley, the under cover man, had left the store, two men walked in, looked at the same radio pretending they wanted to purchase it, and made some inquiries regarding its qualities. They had no sooner left than Constable McDuffie and another man walked in and seized the radio as a smuggled one, as the duty had not been paid. Nemetz saw Handley the same afternoon at the corner of Twelfth street and Victoria drive and told him what had

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
happened, but Handley said to Nemetz to pay the duty and just forget all about it. I am going to ask a question at this point in connection with this case, because I hold in my hand the receipt which was given by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to this man Nemetz. It reads:
Received from Leo Nemetz at New Westminister, B.C., this 23rd day of February, 1934, pending decision, the sum of $44.96, on account of charges against Leo Nemetz, for contravention of the Customs Act.
My question in regard to that would be: Is it the regular procedure of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to seize goods that come in illegally, take the party before them, hold a little court, impose a fine and let him go? That aspect of the matter should be looked into. The serious part of the whole affair however is that this man was permitted to go around freely offering these goods, either cigarettes or moonshine or alcohol or radios, all brought from across the line, and no sooner would he find a victim, shall I say, than information would be sent on to the mounted police who would come along and pick the man up, after which I understand moieties were paid to the informers. I stated the last time I was speaking in regard to this matter and I say again that it looks as if some kind of plot was in progress to build up cases in order to show what wonderful work the mounted police were doing. In speaking about these cases I do not want to be misunderstood or regarded as one who is ready to besmirch the good name of the mounted police. I think the cases I have mentioned besmirch their name without my doing it, and I might say in British Columbia the word of these men is not now being accepted by the judiciary. In fact this man Handley was called "a blatant liar" by the judge in the court, which is very strong language for a judge to use against any man.
I have before me another case with which I am not going to deal. Kemp and another man had guns taken away from them at the border where they had some alcohol in their car. Working for the mounted police they had two other men covered and were going to arrest them when a farmer opened the door of his house, pointed a shotgun at the two of them and took the gun off each. That matter was the subject of a little bit oi ridicule and it did not enhance the reputation of the mounted police in any way.
Did they get their guns back?

I am not sure whether they
did. I think the cases I have mentioned are serious enough to warrant some investigation
or inquiry being made. I am one of those who believe the duty of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is not to go around looking for bottles of whisky or offering liquor to people in order to sell it to them and afterwards report them. We have municipal and provincial police handling liquor cases, and fairly efficiently, I believe. I say from experience that never yet have the mounted police cooperated in any way with the municipal police. As a matter of fact when I was reeve of a municipality and we endeavoured to get their cooperation, we were told that their work was secret and no tips or information could be given out to the municipal police, but they would be glad to get all the tips and information possible from the municipal police. I say that in all seriousness because as I mentioned a few moments ago I have had personal experience of their operations. I think the method of all this secret work and all these under cover men should be looked into, and the whole system readjusted and put on a better footing. We had a case not long ago of one member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who joined the ranks of the communists and obtained information. If they have regular men on the force who can do that they shoud have regular men who can look after contraband or excise in a proper way. But when they hire men with no reputation at all, whose word no one would believe on a stack of bibles, men who are wanted for crime in other countries and have come to this country under questionable conditions, and knowledge of these facts is given to the mounted police and little done about it, I think the committee will agree that the situation is serious indeed. My view is that if the Royal Canadian Mounted Police paid more attention to dope running, especially on ships coming from the orient to Vancouver or New Westminster, instead of all this activity in regard to liquor, it would be more to the general advantage.
I would like to know whether this man Handley is now in gaol or whether he has been deported. Also the total moieties paid to these men. I do not think that should be considered secret. Also, did the mounted police pay the court expenses of these men Handley and Kemp? Handley could not raise the fine anyway, and I understand he was put in gaol, but whether he is there at present I do not know. In view of the fact that these under cover men are in touch with United States interests, are able to obtain gallons of liquor or moonshine or gin, bring it back into British Columbia, offer it to others so that they may go into

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
the business, and then immediately report them to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I cannot find words strong enough to condemn such a system. In my opinion these practices should be absolutely stopped, and until the municipal or provincial police call on the mounted police for assistance to carry on what is the ordinary police work I think they should stay outside the municipalities and not be carrying on this work and without the. knowledge of the authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have listened with a
great deal of interest to the statement by my hon. friend, and I regret to say that I cannot defend the actions of the two men that he has been discussing here this afternoon. Some weeks ago my hon. friend gave me an intimation that he was going to discuss the cases of Handley and Tufts alias Kemp, and I had inquiry made and a report prepared in regard to them. I have to admit that in these instances, out of our force of some 2,500 or 2.600 men, we did unfortunately get two black sheep. Handley was taken on as an agent, I think for about three months. The other man never was on the strength in any way, shape or form, but was evidently what they call a spotter, and he received some portion of the fines which were imposed in the cases with which he dealt, which we call a moiety of the fine. I am sorry I have no record of the amount that he received in that respect. We have to write to British Columbia to get that. I shall endeavour to get the figures for my hon. friend.
The mounted police in British Columbia have but a limited jurisdiction, similar to what they have in Ontario and Quebec. In the other provinces they are the police force of the province under agreement with the province, but not so in British Columbia. In that province the duty of the mounted police simply is to see to the enforcement of the Excise Act, the Customs Act, the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, and any other dominion act that they may specially be required to enforce. But they have nothing to do with the enforcement of the ordinary criminal law of the country or of the provincial liquor law. This man Handley was employed as a secret agent without knowledge of his past history. It is true that after three months' experience with this man he was arrested with his running mate, Tufts, on charges laid against them by the local police, and was condemned to a fine of . $500 with alternative of six months in gaol. Both of these men I understand are now serving their term of imprisonment. My information is that the department took no

part in their defence whatever, paid no money for it, and was not in any way connected with it. I think for the information of the committee I had better read the report. It is largely in corroboration of the statements I have already made, but it is not very long:
With regard to Handley, before he became a paid agent of the force, he apparently had sold to or purchased liquor from Wong Sam.
After becoming a paid agent in this force, he caused a seizure of illicit liquor to be made under the Excise Act from Wong Sam.
Whilst the excise ease above referred to was before the courts, the provincial police of British Columbia took action against Handley with respect to the first transaction referred to in this memorandum in the dealings between Handley and Wong Sam.
Immediately Handley's action with Wong Sam was brought to light through the charge by the provincial police, Handley was dismissed from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
In so far as Handley is concerned, before he was engaged by the mounted police, enquiries were made respecting his record in Canada and United States, but no enquiries were made in England or Australia, although Handley was questioned respecting his record in those countries. He not only lied to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but also to his own counsel, Mr. L. H. Jackson, and therefore his criminal record in those countries was unknown to the force, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police admit that in these particulars, his record was not fully investigated, and that he should not have been employed.
Emphasis is placed upon the fact that Handley had committed his wrong-doing before he actually became a paid agent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and he was immediately dismissed as a result of the charge by the British Columbia provincial police.
With regard to Tufts, alias Kemp, this man was not a paid agent of the force, but was simply an informer who had been giving independent information and for which he was paid separately in each instance.
For the past seven years, he had' supplied information to the preventive service on a moiety basis.
The charges against Handley and' Tufts under the British Columbia Liquor Control Act was disposed of and both accused were convicted by Police Magistrate Darling at Brighotise. B.C., on April 28, 1934, the maximum penalty of $500 fine or, in default, six months' imprisonment being imposed in each instance. The sentences were appealed but the convictions were upheld.
My information is that both men are still in custody. Now the greatest care is taken in the selection of men for the mounted police force. All possible precautions are taken in regard to the history and conduct of men who are taken on, but occasionally we have one put over on us, just as in other businesses. In this case I am satisfied that we had two highly undesirable men, one taken on the force and the other used on the moiety basis

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
as set out in that report. I think their conduct was infamous; as soon as it was discovered they were both cast adrift, and are now in prison after prosecution by the local police.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police do not interfere with the local police; their sole duty is to look after the revenues of the crown in regard to customs and excise, but as my hon. friend knows there are occasions when the city police call upon them for assistance. Many times in Vancouver, sometimes in Toronto and sometimes in Montreal they have been called upon by the civic authorities, and they are always very ready to give their assistance when so called upon, but they do not interfere with the operations of the municipal or provincial police in these provinces.
The question of the employment of under cover men in connection with liquor cases is one upon which there are evidently two opinions. For instance, in the province of Manitoba where the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have authority as provincial police, the provincial liquor board maintains from twelve to fifteen under cover men, plain-ciothesmen, simply for the purpose of seeing to the enforcement of the liquor act of that province; that is their business. The mounted police operate in the same way, but they not only seek to enforce the liquor act of the province of Manitoba; they look after the dominion customs and excise laws also. We look after the work altogether in Saskatchewan and in Alberta; in the maritime provinces also the enforcement of the provincial laws is in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. For the purpose of enforcing provincial acts it always has been the custom-, I believe, to employ plainclothesmen, inspectors, spotters or whatever you may call them. They do it in Ontario, where they have a host of them; I think they use them in [DOT]Quebec also, but in the maritimes and in two of the western provinces that work is left to the mounted police. That is looking after the retail end of the business, if it may be so called; it is not in connection with the revenues of the dominion but in connection with the revenues of the liquor board of the province. It is- a custom that has prevailed throughout Canada, I believe, and in the United States and England for many years. Special means have to be adopted to prevent the illicit sale of liquor and to prevent breaches of provincial or dominion liquor laws. Occasionally a case of hardship arises; occasionally a case of wrongdoing arises, as in the cases cited this afternoon, but on the
whole the system has not worked badly; on the whole smuggling has been pretty well checked up, though not stopped by any means. Excise has been pretty well collected, though breaches of the laws still continue. I think it is the desire of everyone that the laws of the land, whether provincial or dominion, should be enforced to the limit, and for the purpose of enforcement, particularly in regard to liquor laws, plainclothesmen, stool pigeons, spotters or whatever you wish to call them have been employed, I think, for generations. They are still employed. Whether or not the practice should be continued I am not going to say, but I regret that I have to state that in the cases of the men mentioned in British Columbia, their records were bad. They put it over the police badly when they were taken on, but their services were dispensed with as soon as their records were known, and I am glad to say they are both in gaol now paying the penalty.

The minister said it was unfortunate these two men had been engaged, but I wrould direct his attention to the fact that this kind of thing is not yet finished. There are other men under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police operating now through the valley, doing exactly the same thing, men with reputations just as bad as Handley's.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Can my hon. friend furnish me with their names?
Yes, I will.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend need not do it openly; he might be good enough to do it by letter.

I certainly will; I will give
the names and the cases, where men are doing exactly the same thing. From the statement of the minister one would almost infer that after these cases were drawn to the attention of the police this practice had ceased, but that has not been the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I did not say that.
The practice of engaging men of no character, to carry on the business that was carried on by Handley and Kemp-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is these men of no character and no principles, who adopt unfair methods, that we want to know about, and if my hon. friend will give me the names I will look into the matter.

I will take the first opportunity to give the minister the names, cases and full particulars. These men are inciting people to purchase moonshine, bottle and label and sell it, and later the Royal Canadian

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
Mounted Police come along and pick them up. I have a case under my hand which occurred this year, which I will pass on to the minister. The hon. gentleman spoke of the necessity of stool pigeons, and I should like to make this suggestion. There are municipal, provincial and mounted police in the province of British Columbia, though the mounted police have not the same responsibility they have in other provinces. Could not many of these men be used? Their work is police work they are men of some character, and only a few of them are known outside Vancouver. Of the two or three hundred men you have in Vancouver could you not occasionally send out different men through the valley? Why take men whose word is no good at all? One of the serious objections we make is that it is not the Excise Act they are endeavouring to enforce. According to my understanding the Excise Act would apply if a man brought kegs or barrels or tins of liquor across the line in contravention of the customs act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the Excise Act has
to do with illegal manufacture.
There is some distinction between keeping unsealed liquor, which is under a provincial act, and keeping contraband.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a good deal of distilling going on that is illegal, and that is an excise matter. Bringing liquor illegally into the country is a customs matter, perhaps an excise matter also. Primarily, however, excise has to do with manufacturing in Canada, distributing in Canada or having in possession illicit liquor.

I know in regard to stool pigeons it has been the common practice

for one municipality-to ask a neighbouring municipality for the loan of a policeman who would not be known to the person suspected, and in most cases they have been able to obtain the necessary evidence and conviction. I suggest to the minister that the regular men in the police force should be used. If things were very bad you could bring a man from Calgary or you could use provincial or municipal police. But at present I maintain there is no cooperation between the mounted police and the municipal police. They work independently of each other; that was why these men were picked up. The municipal police were not aware that these men were in the pay of the mounted police. I would plead with the minister that instructions be sent out to see that there is more cooperation with the municipal police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We extend all the cooperation we can, but we have to receive a request before we can do anything. The instances which I cited were all instances in which we had direct requests either from the heads of the municipal police or from the attorney general.

I will be glad to send the
information to the minister.

The hon. member for New Westminster has opened up a question which is so wide in its ramifications that it extends far beyond his province, and perhaps it is something that he does not altogether appreciate or understand. It applies to every province in the Dominion of Canada; it applies to every place in the United Kingdom or in the British dominions where the question of detection by police officers is considered in respect of any breach of the law.
The hon. member for New Westminster has addressed to the Minister of Justice a number of questions in connection with the behaviour of certain men who have been members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the minister in that frank and straightforward way which is one of his outstanding characteristics-
Hear, hear.
Is there anyone who challenges that?
No; wo say "Hear, hear."

It was challenged yesterday, but to-day we are having a stag party. The minister has stated that no encouragement has been given to the men who in the name of the law are misconducting themselves in that province. That is an important point, but it is by no means the most important.
The most important question which may come before this parliament or before any other body charged with the duty of enforcing laws is as to whether or not we may get into that system, that very discredited system, of having men employed by government officials or by government organizations acting in the capacity of what the French call agents provocateurs, men who feel that there are weak persons in a community who, although having no intention of committing a criminal breach of a law, if approached and subjected to the suggestion that it might be to their advantage to become criminals, to that extent would lend themselves to such a suggestion in the hope that they might profit by it.

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
A number at least of those persons to whom the hon. member for New Westminster has referred are apparently persons who have been approached in that manner. Quite a number of years ago this particular question was discussed in a number of leading cases in England. The late Mr. Justice Armour, son of the great Chief Justice Armour, who unhappily died just about a year ago, made a collection of cases which in the last few moments I have tried to obtain from the library, but upon which so far I have not been able to place my hands. The sum total of what was investigated and considered in the highest courts of the British empire was this, that if you know a man is planning to commit a breach of a criminal law there is nothing wrong in, shall I say, leading him on to commit that offence which in any event he intends to commit. You may put him legitimately in such a position whereby whilst in the commission of the offence he may be taken in flagrante delicto and made to pay the full penalty for what he has done..
How different that is from going to a man who is known to have poor resistance, perhaps almost of weak mentality, but for whatever reason at all events is exposed to a maximum of temptation with a minimum of resistance, and inducing him to commit a crime he never contemplated, one which found its being in the mind of a police officer who has found this man an easy subject and who has said to himself, "If I can induce that man to commit the crime I will profit by promotion, or otherwise, and thereby increase my personal advantage."
It seems to me the great point to be considered whether it be in connection with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the provincial police, the municipal police or any other police body is that this parliament shall not only not tolerate but shall look with abhorrence upon the act of any person who conducts himself in that way, with an idea of inducing a man to commit a crime in order that a certain police officer may profit by so inducing the man, and then arresting him and making him pay the penalty. If I follow correctly the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster at least three or four of the incidents he related to the committee were as I have indicated. If they were, no condemnation could be too strong for them. If they were, no steps that this parliament could take would be too drastic to put an end to that sort of thing. If the hon. member has suggested to the committee that that has been the animating motive behind the mounted police who have operated in British Columbia,
then I suggest that all other possibilities of investigation into police activities which have been mentioned pale beside the necessity for an investigation of this evil.
It has been stated over an over again, and unhappily I am foroed to believe it, that the mounted police in Canada have at times been employed in approaching unfortunate drug addicts who, with their craving for morphia or heroin have been unable to resist the suggestion that they should obtain it by any means in their power. The police have egged them on to take the drug and then have made arrests, sending those people to prison. I would like to think this is not so, but the suggestions that such things have happened are very strong, very positive and have been repeated many times. I am glad to note that the government has seen fit to allow an investigation into the activities of that body, and I hope when that investigation takes place this particular branch will not be neglected. I hope that the canker worm that has apparently crept into the activities of that body in British Columbia will be found on investigation not to have extended to other provinces. But may I suggest to the hon. Minister of Justice, who is ever alert to stop abuses and to protect the rights of those who are affected by them that he can serve no more useful purpose than in determining in any investigation that may be undertaken in the near future whether or not those abuses of which my hon. friend from New Westminster has spoken have travelled, so to speak, under the surface of the ground into other provinces as well. I think the hon. member for New Westminster is to be commended for bringing a matter of this kind to the notice of the house, and I only hope that the department of which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is the honoured head will see that any investigation to be undertaken shall be thorough and comprehensive, that, these abuses shall exist nowhere else.

If the hon. member for
West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) is ready to act as investigator with the same solemnity as he spoke just now, may I urge his appointment upon the minister?

Mr. Chairman, fortunately I represent a constituency where the police force have very little to do. We settle our cases among ourselves, and I have no complaint against the mounted police. On the contrary, every time I have come in contact with them I have been very pleased with the courtesy they have shown me. I would be the last one in this house to raise any prejudice or any cry of race or language

Supply-Justice-Mounted Police
or anything of that kind, but I should like to refer to the celebration that took place in Gaspe last year of the four hundredth anniversary of the discovery of Canada. I heard quite a number of remarks about the inability of the mounted police who were there to answer in French questions that were put to them for information. I suppose that in this able body there are a number of French-speaking officers. I have no objection whatever to the high officials of the mounted police, who of course have not very much to do with the French-speaking population, being English-speaking, but on an occasion such as that at Gaspe last year it seems to me that it should have been foreseen that we would have a very distinguished gathering from France, and in fact, Mr. Chairman, it was perhaps one of the most distinguished delegations that has ever visited this continent from France. These people came to that celebration with the idea of meeting on the spot French-speaking people and Frenchspeaking officers, but the impression that was created upon them was the contrary of what one might have expected. I say that not in any spirit of complaint because I know that the festivities were organized in somewhat of a hurry, and I do appreciate very much the good order that was established within a few days in the nice little city of Gaspe, but I think that when a celebration like that takes place in the future a little consideration should be given to the aspect of the question that I have mentioned. As I said at the outset, it is with a little reluctance that I bring this matter up here at all, but it is from a sincere desire to avoid in the future remarks such as I heard on that occasion.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: No; there are no charges on any ships going through the canal.

There should be a tax on these ships, and I make that suggestion to the government; it has already been made. There is no reason why foreign ships passing through Canadian canals should not pay a tax. This is a humble suggestion I offer the government. The hon. gentleman complains that he gets no suggestions from this side. This is one. We have to bear the whole burden of taxation, and I think that ships of foreign registration, enjoying the same facilities as ships registered in Canada, should be taxed.

There is no doubt that the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman has been considered from time to time. Last year we had a lengthy debate in the house on this very question; in fact, the whole question of tolls on canals was debated on the motion, if I remember rightly, of the hon. member for M-uskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon). Unfortunately it was found-and I looked into the question thoroughly at that time-that the practice of levying tolls, up to about 1904, had not been a paying proposition. As regards charging a toll on foreign vessels alone, the question has been looked into from the standpoint of treaty rights, international obligations and so on, and it has been found that we cannot charge tolls on foreign vessels without also levying them on Canadian ships, owing to international agreements which Canada has with other countries. I cannot give the details at the moment, but that is the fact. Even when tolls were charged, about thirty years ago, the income was so small that' it was not of sufficient importance to warrant charging them, and it had the effect at that time, as it would have again, of
diverting a great deal of traffic down through the Erie canal and New York instead of through Montreal and Canadian ports. I am sure the hon. gentleman makes the suggestion in good faith, buit we have looked into the matter thoroughly, as have past governments, and it was considered by past governments as well as by this administration that the proposal is not feasible.

There are five or six items to provide for settlement of claims in connection with contracts dating back some years ago. How were these settlements reached? Were these contracts the subject of litigation, or were there arbitrations?

There are altogether seven or eight claims and we are now dealing with the last one. These companies received construction contracts during the past twenty years in connection with the Welland ship canal, and I believe that most of them were given by the late government or the one that preceded it.
Most of them by the last government.

Yes; I merely-mention
that as a matter of fact. These contracts were for huge amounts. The first item, No. 84, concerns a contract with the J. P. Porter Company. That contract was for $11,376,000, and I think it goes back to about 1924 or 1925. It was for a substantial amount of work on the Welland ship canal in accordance with unit prices, and when we came in we simply carried on the contracts. I do not think there were any changes of importance. When the Porter company had completed their work-and this applies to all these settlements-they put in claims for extras amounting to a little over $571,000. These claims were later revised, being reduced to $384,000; and after a discussion with the engineers, going into each case very completely, I came to the decisions which are indicated here. The original claim of $571,000 in the case of the Porter company was cut down to a final settlement of $110,000, though the amount shown here is not $110,000 but $89,000 odd, the difference consisting in settlements which could be made in connection with unit work or something of that sort. It was considered that in this, as in the other instances, the company had an equitable claim to the amount decided upon, representing the difference between the legal claim and the other. Without naming the other companies, it might be interesting to give the amounts of the original claim in

each instance together with the final settlement. There is a claim for $250,000, settled for $9,800; a claim for $828,000 settled for $40,000; a claim for $63,000, settled for $18,000; a claim for $393,000, settled for $50,000; a claim for $126,000-not quite $127,000-settled for $20,000; a claim foT $1,288, settled for $939. The last one, with which I had nothing to do, was settled by the officers themselves. It was for $3,000 and was settled for $1,500. So that the settlements were exceedingly satisfactory; in fact, I do not mind saying that most of the companies made strong complaints.

Does this
complete the construction cost of the Welland canal or are there still some items outstanding?

We have a small amount
for the Robertson company-No. 87-and they have not settled. The Robertson company have put in a claim for $393,000 altogether and our item is S37,000 odd. When we were making the settlements, being anxious to dispose of all of them, we found that the manager or president, or whoever the responsible official of the company was, was not in the country. The official who the company felt should deal with the matter for them was in Europe and therefore did not discuss it with the engineers. Therefore that is not a settlement, but we have put in a figure that covers what we consider is their legal claim. Most of them are settled except in the case of a couple of companies, one being the Peter Lyall Company about which my hon. friends opposite know something and the ex-Minister of Railways would know a good deal. They make a rather heavy claim in regard to some alterations in labour prices. The contracts stated that they were awarded on the basis of certain labour prices and the Labour department of the former government raised the wages. The Peter Lyall people have put in a claim amounting to something like half a million dollars; I am speaking again from memory. This was submitted to Mr. Justice Maclean, not as a regular case but for his opinion. He gave a sort of umpire's decision rather favourable to the Lyall people, but the matter has not yet been settled, and it has not been included in any of the settlements here. Outside the Lyall claim and some others that might be contingent upon a settlement of the Lyall claim on the same grounds, I believe most of the claims have been settled. By the way the total cost of the Welland ship canal is in round figures $130,000,000; I thought somebody might ask for it.

For how long are the international agreements? Those are the agreements signed whereby ships from the United States and other foreign countries can go through the canal free.

I should have said international trade treaties; they are full treaties. Perhaps I used the word "agreement " wrongly. They are treaties between Canada and such countries as for instance Holland. I remember that the ships of Holland were drawn to my attention as those upon which tolls should be paid. In looking into the matter I found that the number of vessels coming from foreign countries apart from the United States were so few that the tolls would not amount to anything substantial. Our canals to-day will permit vessels only 250 feet in length to traverse them, except the Welland ship canal which is built midway between the others so that it was rather an unwise piece of building without extending the depth and length of all the other canals in unison with it. But it was begun some twenty-two years ago and it has been carried on by every government since that time, with the exception of a short period during the war, so that it was practically a continuous affair.
It was a continuing sin.
