Under this item perhaps I may bring to the attention of the committee a grievance of our section of the country that has existed for some years, namely the disuse of the national transcontinental from Quebec to Winnipeg. I listened very attentively some days ago to an hon. member from British Columbia urging preferential freight rates to the Pacific coast. But the same arguments apply more forcibly to that section of the Canadian National line from Quebec to Winnipeg. I brought this matter before the house when I was sitting on the government side and on several occasions since. So far not only have we not had these complaints remedied by the present government or the board of railway commissioners, but services have been further curtailed. Through passenger service is nil. In the spring of 1931, after this present government took office, there was curtailment of the passenger service so well given by trains Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4, and to-day the Canadian National has entirely lost all that traffic in that section. And since 1929 we have not had any through freight service. This line is really the missing link as far as the national railways are concerned. I make this appeal to the committee for the very good reason that it is useless to make it to the railway commission; we have tried that in the past, so the last court to which we can appeal is this committee and the Minister of Railways. I appreciate the statement made by the minister a few days ago that he is not in favour of amalgamation, but so far as the national transcontinental in our section is concerned there has been a thorough process of elimination. Within a few years the rails will be rusted and the line useless on account of absence of traffic which that road is absolutely entitled to have.
I do not think this is the time or place to review the past history of that part of our railway system, but every hon. member is familiar with the fact that there are no better grades on any railway in this country. More than that, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier introduced the legislation to provide for the national transcontinental on July 30, 1903, speaking of the link covering the northern section of Ontario and Quebec he used these words:
This new railway will be another link in that chain of union. It will not only open territory hitherto idle and unprofitable, it will

not only force Canadian trade into Canadian channels, it will not only promote citizenship between old' Canada and new Canada, but it will secure us our commercial independence, and will forever make us free from the bondage of the bonding privilege.
I well remember only a few years ago commending the present minister when he severely criticized the condition under which our grain was finding its way to American seaports for export. Although this is not the case in such large volume now, because we do not export so much grain, nevertheless the fact remains that a large quantity of all grains is still finding its way to the ports of the United States, while at the same time we have one of the finest sections of the Canadian National system absolutely idle. More than that, I believe that the present government is responsible for a certain amount of prejudice against our section. Only a few weeks ago I was reading an editorial in an Ottawa paper in which the question was asked, Why use that section of railway, passing through a country that produces only Christmas trees? Let me remind the committee that the northern sections of Ontario and Quebec are among the very richest in our country. I should like to see some of those writers try to cut down some of these small "Christmas trees." We have in -my riding alone three great newsprint mills, at Iroquois Falls, Smooth Rock Falls and Kapuskasing.
It takes more than Christmas trees to keep them going. When by the national transcontinental that section of the country was opened up we made a great capital investment. I am sure that no section of our population begrudged the building of that railway. But a certain amount of prejudice has been fastened on our section on account of the attitude of the present government. We fervently hope and expect that the passenger service on the national transcontinental will be reestablished. I am not a railway man but I am told by people well versed in the matter that as far as that line is concerned, through the discontinuance of the service since 1931 by the national trains from Quebec to Winnipeg, they have practically lost all the through passenger traffic that they had. Furthermore I am positive that they have lost all the through passenger traffic going west from our own section of the country, because the people resent the fact that that service has been cut off, and when people from Cochrane and Kapuskasing and neighbouring towns want to go west they have to go a roundabout way. I believe the statement cannot be contradicted that as far as our section of the country is concerned all the

Supply-Railway Commission
passenger traffic has been lost to the Canadian Pacific. If that is cooperation it is not the kind we believe in. We fully realize that there is a railway problem, and that problem is too great to be dealt with on party lines. We fully realize that every hon. member must give that question his most careful and intelligent consideration. But I maintain that as far as the national transcontinental is concerned it never came into its own, it never got a chance. From the time it was built to the present day the rates have been discriminatory. For instance when the road was completed in 1916 it was able to quote a rate of six cents per bushel on wheat from Armstrong, a station in the Thunder Bay district almost due north of Fort William and Port Arthur, to Quebec city, a distance of 959 miles. Then something very mysterious happened. After it w'as shown by actual test that grain or cattle could be hauled more economically on that section of the road than on any other section, discriminatory rates were instituted against us; as a matter of fact the rates proved to be not only discriminatory but practically prohibitive, and as a result the expected volume of traffic did not develop and has not developed since. In 1931 the Quebec harbour commission made representations to the board of railway commissioners complaining about the rate of 20-7 cents per bushel from Armstrong to Quebec. An investigation was held by the board in Quebec city, with the late Hon. Frank Car-vell presiding, and during that hearing there were certainly some very extraordinary arguments advanced. Here is the verbatim comment of Mr. Carvell:
If my conception of the national transcontinental was right, when it was started and when it was being built, I think freight can be transported over that line at a figure which would mean the absolute ruination of other railways in Canada. If not, we were all wrong and we were not justified in building it.
So it seems a very strange anomaly indeed, in these times of the new deal, that we do not take the line of least resistance and that the railway commission do not find it possible to have all our grain routed over that section of the road, at least during the winter months, since at the present time that line is being used only for local traffic.
It is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the house; I believe the people throughout the country are fully seized of the problem. This also hurts the maritimes. There are many members on both sides of the house coming from the maritime provinces who have deplored the fact that the harbours of Saint John and
Halifax have not received their proper quota of through traffic. That is due to the fact that millions of bushels of wheat have been shipped through United States ports each year. Those are the latest statistics I have been able to obtain. No doubt the decrease in the amount of grain exported through those ports is due to the fact that our exports of grain in general have not been as great for some years past. I maintain that every bushel of that grain should have been carried over our Canadian railways, because if my information is correct this grain was all shipped during the winter months, when our railways and our water transportation systems on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence have not been carrying on that business. In this way our section of the country, together with the maritime provinces, have been cheated out of a great deal of revenue. If the eleven cent rate to Quebec were effective, immediately it would create a maximum rate on the great lakes. I do not know why these discriminatory rates in our section have been maintained during the winter months; I could understand it more easily if they were even seasonal rates. We in the north are fair enough to realize that railway transportation from the west to the maritimes could not compete with water transportation, but we maintain that at least during the winter months all grain hauled should go over that section of the railway.
Grain is not the only commodity that can be moved more expeditiously over that line. A few years ago a trial shipment of 600 steers was sent over that railway, and the running time of the train between Winnipeg and Quebec was eighteen hours less than the running time from Winnipeg to Montreal. Two feedings were sufficient where three were required in the other case, and this, together with a smaller shrinkage in the shipment, represented a saving of not less than $5 per head or of roughly S3,000 on the consignment. But that experiment was conducted only
Supply-Railway Commission

once; we have never had any other through traffic in cattle, though I do not know why.
It has been stated in my section of the country, as well as in northern Quebec, the city of Quebec and the maritime provinces, that the Canadian National have not been given a fair chance. I do not believe there is proper cooperation between the two railways. I absolutely agree with the minister when he says we cannot have amalgamation, but it is a good thing to have this question before the public at the present time. I would remind the government that there has been almost a united effort on the part of some hon. members opposite to suggest that the Canadian National system is not an asset to the country, but that it is such a load that it would be a wonderful thing if it could be given away or sold for five dollars. This is not good for the country or for the railway system. A few moments ago we passed estimates amounting to several millions of dollars in connection with the Welland canal, and the minister mentioned a large sum that was to be spent on the Rideau canal. In the last few years we have also made other capital investments such as the railway to Churchill and the terminal there. These are not paying propositions, but I a.m sure no hon. member would suggest that they should not have been built. So I am sure no member of parliament, no matter on what side of the house he sits, would suggest that the transcontinental line should not have been built. If he knows the development that has taken place in that section of the country, which has proved so beneficial to the whole of Canada, he would realize that these expenditures were fully warranted. In my own section of the country through the gold tax alone the federal government have collected something over $4,000,000. That is only one item, and it shows the potential assets, some of which have been developed, in that section of the country. ,
The house should be fully seized of the necessity of maintaining the integrity of the road. I realize that it would be impossible for the minister to say that the Canadian Northern system should be destroyed. Everyone knows that with the scattered population strung along that section of the road such a declaration would arouse horror in every section of the country. But if there is a section of the system which should be abolished it is that section instead of the transcontinental, for the very good reason that the transcontinental travels through the famous clay belt of northern Quebec and northern Ontario, while the Canadian North-
[Mr. Bradette.l
ern is in between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. In our section we maintain that because of the policy that has been followed in connection with the transcontinental we have lost the traffic to which we were entitled.
I have mentioned these facts because I wish to make a very sincere appeal to the minister that he use his influence with the railway commission to have the situation remedied. The commission is not a political body; in our section of the country when we deal with these matters, particularly railway matters, we always keep out of the realm of politics. I hope I may receive the support of hon. members from northern Quebec and northern Ontario, because I think we all realize that instead of being an asset to that section of the country the transcontinental has become a liability because it has not received the consideration it deserves. I am not going to give any further statistics at the present time; I need only say that the rates on grain and cattle are nearly double the rates on other sections of the line. Is that fair to the Canadian National railways as a whole? Is that fair to northern Ontario and northern Quebec? Is it fair to the maritime provinces? I will say it is not. It is not giving a chance to that system in connection with the building of which the founders were looking to the future. This traffic has been taken from our section of the country and we are not receiving the just-treatment we might expect. We have no direct communication; we are nearly 300 miles northwest of North Bay and have no direct communication with Winnipeg or the western provinces. While we have the very best roadbed on the North American continent, no use is made of it. The province of Quebec, the city of Quebec and the maritime provinces have not ready access, so far as railway facilities are concerned, because they have to go in a roundabout way.
Before concluding my remarks may I make a last appeal to the Minister of Railways. He has resided in northern Ontario and I believe he knows as well as I do the conditions obtaining in that section of the country. He knows that the Canadian National railways have not been treated fairly so far as passenger service to that part of the country is concerned. He knows, too, that ninety-five per cent of the passenger service in northern Ontario is lost to the Canadian National Railways, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway has benefited. The people in my section of the country have no quarrel with the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Supply-Railway Commission
We know it is a national institution and has rendered service to the country, but surely the railway commission and the Minister of Railways should see to it that our railway service is linked up.

I know the hon. member has made what he considers to be a sincere appeal. Usually he is eminently fair, but on this occasion, particularly in regard to the last few sentences, of his observations, I do not think he has been quite fair. For instance, he indicated that the cutting off of passenger traffic on the northern lines of the Canadian National railways was quite unfair to those railways, and stated in so many words that such action favoured the Canadian Pacific Railway. If any unfairness exists so far as the Canadian National railways are concerned, the hon. member must know, as I do, that it has been brought about by their own management, because neither the Minister of Railways of this government nor that of the late government, no matter what the faults of that government may have been, have had anything to do with the actual operation of the railways. I have no control over the train schedules, because ministers of railways are not consulted on those matters. The railway managements, whether they be of the Canadian National or of the Canadian Pacific, handle their own train arrangements. Therefore I submit if any unfairness has been the result it is the fault of the management. I would not agree that the management would be so foolish as to permit themselves to be unfair to themselves

because that is what the hon. member has suggested in his declaration that the conditions obtaining are unfair to the national system. It is an old cry, and I do not think the hon. member is quite fair to himself when he repeats it because the management of the national railways have been handling the road exceedingly well. Were I to show the hon. member a statement of the earnings for the first six weeks of this year or for the whole of last year he would see that the Canadian National Railways is earning in the present year and in the past year did earn considerably greater revenue than the Canadian Pacific Railway did.
I think the Canadian National Railways management are eminently fair to themselves, and no doubt their only reason for taking trains off the northern route was that they do not feel such trains were justified by the earnings. Naturally the management must eliminate services which do not give a reasonable return of revenue. Only last week I visited my own constituency, and as the Canadian National
Railways have no direct train running from Ottawa to Fort William as a matter of convenience I travelled via the Canadian Pacific; I really had no choice in the matter. I went up on train No. 1 and came back on No. 2, trains which used to carry through Pullmans and dining cars but which because of scarcity of traffic through northwestern Ontario do not now provide those facilities on the trains in question. The Canadian Pacific Railway have eliminated many of their trains for the same reason as have the Canadian National Railways.
I do not wish to enter into any lengthy discussion of the railway situation, and for that reason will deal with only one or two further points raised by the hon. member. He has stated that the national railways have not been fair to the northern country, and in an effort to substantiate his arguments he quoted some journals or newspapers which had made certain statements. Surely the hon. member would not suggest that the Department of Railways and Canals must be responsible for everything appearing in a newspaper. Those journals are not our mouthpiece; so far as possible we endeavour to speak for ourselves. He must not forget that traffic on the Canadian National railways in 1933 was less than half of the amount in 1928, the peak year. My memory indicates that in 1928 the gross revenues of the Canadian National railways were about 8300,000.000, while in 1933 they were only about 8148,000,000, or a little less than half. Naturally the same service cannot be given when earnings have been cut in half.
The hon. member made reference to wheat and other traffic which he thought should come down via the northern route. A few moments ago he was kind enough to state that I am from northern Ontario. May I say I am very proud of it, and in my heart I have a strong affection for that particular section of Canada. In area it is huge; in fact without consulting a map one hardly realizes that the northern portion of Ontario is more than five times the area of the more thickly populated southern section -of the province. Unfortunately, however, the population in the greater area is small, and for that reason the passenger revenues from that part of Ontario cannot be heavy. Therefore the hon. member must understand that from the standpoint of passenger traffic there is no justification for heavy or regular passenger services. When the hon. member indicates that wheat and other commodities are not shipped via the northern route may I point out that practically no wheat comes east by rail from Winnipeg. An
24G8

Supply-Railway Commission
odd car may be sent by rail because of some emergency, but practically ail the grain which oomes east from Winnipeg goes first to the head of the lakes and then comes down by water to the Georgian bay ports and Port Co.lborne, or through to Montreal. When it is shipped from the port of New York it goes via Buffalo. I would say however that the vast majority, probably 99^r per cent of all the grain coming east, comes by water simply because the rail rates are about ten times as high as the water rates. I have given the round figure, but I believe I am approximately correct. Obviously there would be no justification for any person shipping by rail when he can ship at one-tenth the cost by water.
There is no hope in the world of my hon. friend's section of the transcontinental line carrying grain to any large extent when in fact that same grain could be shipped at a much lower rate by water. Probably I should modify my general statement to the effect that the rate is ten times as high by rail as by water, because I remember that at one time a special rate became effective from the head of the lakes or from Winnipeg to the city of Quebec. I believe the rate of eleven cents was given, a very low rate, from the city of Fort William to the city of Quebec. However, even that exceedingly low rate did not attract grain traffic to the railways, because the rate by lake and rail, if I remember correctly the figures I gave the other night, from the head of the lakes to Montreal averaged 3-79 during the 1933 season of navigation. Obviously no person would pay eleven cents from Fort William to Quebec if he could ship it from Fort William to Montreal for 3-79 cents. To attempt to carry on a grain traffic by the Canadian National railways or any other railways when that grain could be shipped more cheaply by water would be as hopeless as trying to push water up hill with a sieve.
How would the minister handle the millions of bushels which in every year find their way to the American seaports for exportation?

Practically every bushel of the grain which goes via the American seaports comes from the head of the lakes to Buffalo by water. From Buffalo it goes on via the Erie canal. Sometimes it leaves Buffalo by rail, but never reaches that city by rail, because it could not be handled profitably by rail. The fact is that it goes from the head of the lakes to Buffalo by water, and possibly for the short haul from Buffalo to New York some of it may go by rail,

just as our grain coming east in the summer comes by water from Fort William to Georgian bay ports, and then by rail east, and occasionally it goes as far as Saint John and Halifax by rail, which is a fairly long haul. But practically no grain ever goes from the west to Montreal or Quebec or to New York by rail. It goes principally by water, except perhaps an occasional car for some emergent need. Members who understand the grain trade, my hon. friend, for instance, from West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) I am sure will not find any fault with my general statement that practically every bushel goes by lake and rail.

I do not like to be complaining, and I know this is a very hard time to ask for railway improvements, but I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that our people in Prince Edward Island and those who come to our province complain very much about the service between Sackville and cape Tormentine. We are not complaining at all about the service to Sackville or in fact about the services on the island, because they are fairly good, but there is a short line from Sackville to Tormentine that is not up to the standard of the rest of the railway. That is the gateway of our province, yet the roadbed is not as good as on other sections of the road, and the passenger cars that are used on this section of the line are not in keeping with the traffic that is carried. Just a few days ago the maritime boards of trade met in Saint John, New Brunswick. A representative from our province attended the meeting and he had no trouble at all in getting a resolution passed drawing the attention of the railway authorities to the fact that the equipment and service was inadequate and needs improvement. I am taking this opportunity of bringing the matter to the minister's attention and I hope that he will take it up with the management.

My hon. friend now draws my attention to this matter publicly, but I may say that he has taken it up a number of times privately with me before. But again I must make the same reply that I did to my hon. friend opposite, and that is the reply which the railway management give me. My hon. friend complained that the passenger service was not sufficient for the people in Prince Edward Island and I did take that matter up, at my hon. friend's request, with the management. From what I hear the passenger service could be very much improved, but the railway give the same reply that I had to give to my hon.

However, I shall very gladly draw to the attention of the management the statements which my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Myers) and my hon. friend opposite have made in regard to these services, and submit to the management that they give further consideration to the whole question. There is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I doubt very much if I can finish before the dinner recess but I will begin. It concerns a number of engine men in the constituency of St. Boniface and in some of the Winni-pegs, and it is really a very important matter. The minister is quite familiar with it, I am sure, as he has received a good many communications from one person or another, but still there seems to be no means olf remedying this festering sore, and the present situation is certainly very unfair to a considerable number of engine men in that terminus.
The facts are these. When the roads that form the Canadian National Railways were amalgamated, so far as Winnipeg is concerned, there were three roads that entered into the amalgamation. There was the old Canadian Northern railway, the terminus of which was in Fort Rouge, a portion of the city of Winnipeg. There was the Canadian government railway running east from Transcona, and there was the Grand Trunk Pacific running west from Transcona. The old Canadian Northern railway engines that were being used at that time were the old fashioned smaller type, hauling only about one-third of the tonnage that the large engines could haul that were being used on the two roads running east and west out of the town of Transcona.
It was found after the roads were amalgamated that a great deal of the traffic was routed east over the former Canadian government lines and that the engineers of the Canadian Northern were getting very little
to do. This condition was aggravated by the fact that that road was in very, very bad condition, and in order to bring it into running shape after the amalgamation of the roads, some fifty crews were put to work on the Canadian Northern railway, which already had very many more engine men working than either the Canadian government road or the Grand Trunk Pacific. There was an agitation set on foot by the engine men of the Canadian Northern portion of the road for equalization or for priority rights with regard to running. I believe it was in 1926 that the matter was taken up through their grand lodge in Cleveland. I have grown a little rusty on the matter but my memory is that committees were appointed by both the engineers and the firemen and that the committees included the presidents and six vice presidents of the labour organizations.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (East Toronto) moved the second reading of Bill No. 50, to amend the Post Office Act (newspaper ownership).
He said: I would not make any remarks on the motion for the second reading of this bill, the passage of which would mean so much to good government in this country, were it not that forty-two per cent of the members of parliament were not in the house when it was brought up. This is the same bill that was passed several years ago by this parliament, agreed to unanimously in the interests of the real freedom of the press. At that time the bill went over to the senate but was rejected. It has been the law of England and of the United States as well for many years.
The war wrought a great change in the democratic conception of education, and we find that the press has been the leader in every phase of life; in fact, I do not know how we should have got along -without the press during the last few years of depression. Now what I want to point out is that in every other department of our activities, whether it be personal estate or real estate, bills of sale, chattel mortgages, wills, municipal assessment for real estate, anyone can go to the assessment office or to the municipality

Post Office Act-Newspapers
and ascertain the facts. Why therefore should we throw a cloak of secrecy around the identity of any newspaper? Everyone knows who the members of the House of Commons are, who the senators are and who the governor general is. Everyone can find out who the directors of all incorporated companies are, whether federal or provincial, because all this information has to be registered. There have to be elaborate statements with affidavits regarding the financial affairs of every corporation. But the income tax dodgers and the newspapers whose identity is not disclosed operate under cover.
There never was a time in the history of the country when it was so imperative as it is to-day that we should know the identity of every newspaper, when we consider the agitation that is going on throughout the country, among certain people, for the amalgamation of the railways and union government; when we consider the fact that the natural resources of the country have been given away to favourites; and when we consider the new deal which has been introduced into this parliament and which, since the opening of this session, the three parties have supported.
Take the investigation by the mass buying commission; that most important subject is related to the proposal put forward in this bill. At the basis of all corruption in this country, since confederation, we find a section of the press which has set itself above this parliament and above the law of the land, large mergers and combines in restraint of trade having operated to control that section of the press. Mr. Stanley Baldwin stated the other day that reform, legal, constitutional and parliamentary, transcended any other problem in importance. We admire the British press and we admire the Canadian press to-day; on the whole it is a splendid institution, and I have no criticism to make of it. I submit however that we shall have to do something to secure for the workers and the people of the country generally what Theodore Roosevelt tried to do years ago for the American people, namely, to give them a square deal, and the "new freedom" which Woodrow Wilson proposed to give them. So that in the interests of improved social, political and economic conditions it is desirable that we should know who they are that control the press. In some of the cities of this country we find two rival newspapers published in the same building and by the sarhe publisher, one Liberal and one Conservative, and no one knows the identity of either paper or whether

some of the editorials are paid for or not. In Canada to-day, as in Britain, all questions of public concern, whether political, economic, constitutional, social, religious or personal are discussed in the press quite freely, without fear or favour or any danger of criminal prosecution-a condition far different from that which existed in England in the eighteenth century when Wilkes was prosecuted. Except for abnormal circumstances, the press can publish anything, good, bad or indifferent, affecting any government or individual. The press is so much a part of the British constitution that we are apt to forget the part it played in securing the benefits we enjoy to-day in connection with our free schools, factory legislation and other important measures of social reform. It has been the standard bearer of freedom. Canada cannot get along without an unfettered press, and a free press is of inestimable advantage to the people of this country. It is a joy to the individual; it illumines the home and exalts the nation, and the saying that "worth makes the man," is applicable to all our great newspaper editors.
Section 1 of the bill provides that there shall be a sworn statement of names and addresses of editors, owners, stockholders, and so forth, to be made semi-annually. Now I submit that inasmuch as they use the post office they should register; the identity of every newspaper should be known. The post office of this country carries second class mail for the newspapers at a net loss of S8,-000,000. The department cannot afford to pay its employees a decent rate of wages because of the franchises handed to the press. Section 1 does not propose that the names of small stockholders shall be given. It is provided that a copy of the sworn statement made by the newspaper shall be published in the second issue printed next after the filing of the statement with the Postmaster General, and if that provision is not carried out then the newspaper may not use the mails. Further, it is provided that paid editorials shall be marked "advertisement." Why not? Why should any large corporation attack a man like Harry Stevens, after all he has done for the country?-a man who, more than any Lord Shaftesbury, deserves the gratitude of this country, first, for what he did in 1926 when he saved the people $55,000,000 in connection with the customs inquiry, and, secondly, in connection with the price spreads commission. Why should such a man be attacked in the manner in which he was in the past few weeks by some few sections of the press?

It is time the people woke up to the fact that we are living in a fool's paradise. When I was chief magistrate of Toronto, an effort was made to sell the city an antiquated street railway plant and light plant largely antiquated junk, for $32,000,000. What would have been the result if that had gone through? The city would have been bankrupt and there would have been no hydroelectric project such as we have it to-day and we would have had higher carfares and rates for power. The toilers and workers in the cities and the farmers on the farms of Ontario would have been affected. There are a few people in this country who tried to put over that deal on the municipalities of this province; they fought Adam Beck to an early grave, and it is due to the Canadian people, who have had various legislatures since confederation down that have given away our natural resources, that we should have some statement of newspaper ownership. I have before me a letter from the Postmaster General of the United States where a similar bill was introduced on August 24, 1912. After all is said and done, the United States has been the great laboratory since the depression came on; it has tried all kinds of schemes to solve the economic troubles of that country and to pull its people out of the mire. Those schemes have been good, bad and indifferent, but in the result, as any economist can tell, most of the legislation passed there has been for the public benefit and has done something for the workers in that country. This is what the Postmaster General of the United States says:
The present law, embodied in section 537, Postal Laws and Regulations, is printed on the back of the accompanying copy of Form 3526 used by publishers in furnishing the required information. It specifies that publishers must submit not later than the first day of October of each year a statement setting forth the names and addresses of the officers of the publication, the owners and stockholders, etc., and also in the ease of daily newspapers the average number of copies sold or distributed to paid subscribers during the preceding twelve months.
The purpose and intent of the law is to discover the real owners of publications entered as second-class matter and to let the public know who controls the editorial policies of the publication. It has been helpful in many instances where it was necessary to ascertain the actual ownership of publications and has also been beneficial in the case of daily publications which are required to show the average daily paid circulation in correcting the practices of some publishers in representing to advertisers a greater circulation for their publication than actually obtained. The law [DOT]on the whole has been beneficial in its effect.
Post Office Act-Newspapers
The law embodied in paragraph 2 of the above mentioned section, requiring editorial or other reading matter for the publication of which money or other valuable consideration is paid, accepted, or promised to be marked with the word "advertisement," enables readers to determine what is advertising and what is reading matter, and since the advertising portion of publications entered as second-class matter, with certain exceptions, is subject to postage at graduated zone rates, according to distance-
And these rates in the United States which I am going to quote are twice what they are in this country where we had a deficit of $8,000,000.

I will not quote the number of papers whose editors have advocated this legislation. They are mostly Conservative, but there have also been many Liberal newspapers. Let me pay tribute to the Liberal party because in 1919 they introduced this very bill in the house. Hon. Mr. Lemieux, then member for Gaspe, introduced this bill in the house on several occasions, in fact this particular bill formed part of the Liberal platform of 1919. I have to pay tribute to Mr. Lemieux because he copied it from the law of England.
But I will say in conclusion that in the United States we have seen the control of Wall Street which the senate inquiry revealed. In that country Mr. J. Pierpont Morgan is a striking example. He and his partners did not pay a penny of income tax for years, and no one outside the precincts of the house of Morgan was any the wiser. It required a United States senate inquiry to expose this evil practice and a senate inquiry to show how tied and non-identity newspapers had been bought to kill public men who opposed in that country the giving away of their last natural resources. This exposure shocked all America and in fact the whole civilized world.
There was a committee formed of thirteen in my city to put over a union government a few weeks ago, the last thing this government wants, and the people would like to know who is behind that particular move.
I have many papers that I could quote from. This is what I said in the by-election in East Toronto, and I do not take a word back of what I said in that riding:
The Conservative party, the real founders and authors of protection in Canada, should not allow itself to become just an adjunct to great mergers and monopolies and restraints of trade and security company racketeering, and who, as well as great departmental stores, are a law to themselves, and snap their fingers at the government and parliament and any regulations from the law of the land as they crush out the small dealer and starve their employees, and by rural mail delivery and the misuse of mail orders ruin the small towns and villages of the province. We had a milk and gasoline inquiry end in no prosecutions as not within the legislative competence of Canada.
The time has come to stop "pussyfooting" with these cankers in the body politic and reassert the supremacy of parliament, as the first duty of a government is to look after the health and happiness, welfare and prosperity of its people. The Conservative party has done itself credit in the spread' prices, and

Post Office Act-Newspapers
mass buying committee.... But the big interests who have so much weight in all parties are out to kill it as they did the milk and gasoline inquiry and the Beauharnois inquiry, and to put the lid on-and also to kill and destroy any private member who opposes them and drive him out of parliament.
I still stand by those words. I believe the Conservative party and this government have done themselves proud in what they have done in the way of protecting the workers, the consumers and especially the farming industry, because the farmers and the industrial workers of this country are traditionally Conservative; they have been the two branches of this party from 1878 down. They have never faltered in the principle of protection. So when I see some of our leaders attacked as they are by some of the tied press for having brought about these reforms for the benefit of the workers, I believe the time has come to know who owns some of the newspapers. The object of this bill is well known to the press. For many years the newspapers have been coming to parliament and securing privileges. Prior to 1882 newspapers were carried free by the post office. This bill provides for what is already required by law in England, Australia and the United States, that is: a sworn statement of the names and addresses of editors, owners and principal stockholders of every newspaper, magazine, periodical or other publication, to be filed with the postmaster general semiannually. There have been quite a number of newspaper references to this bill. Various farmers' magazines have openly approved the proposed legislation as being in the best interests of a free press and a free parliament. The Farmer's Advocate, the St. Catharines Standard, the Globe and the Port Hope Guide, The Winchester Press, are a few cases in point. I want it understood that I am not for a moment attacking the press of this country; I do not believe you could find anywhere a press to excel it. The contribution which Canadian newspapers made to the community, the country, education, social benefit, the satisfactory outcome of the war and during the depression; what it did to promote the cause of the poor and needy and of charity and philanthropy and to further every worthy movement on behalf of the soldiers and of the nation at large was invaluable and finds its place on the proudest pages of Canada's history. It was the press that helped very largely to restore Canada to her normal position. Nor can one say too much for the honour and integrity of the press of Canada. The tendency of our Canadian newspapers is decidedly forward, and not backward, and notwithstanding the high cost of material and
labour and the depression and the social situation their prospects are bright. I have no doubt that the genius of our newspapers will help to make this country great industrially and socially and in every way, so that Canada will march triumphantly on from strength to strength.
The object of the bill is to require disclosure of ownership so that we know who the owners are. No fair minded man in the country, can oppose this proposal; if he has at heart the interests not only of the country, but of the press itself he will support this bill. For these reasons I move the second reading. Having done that, the onus is on the house. This bill is not a party measure; on a former occasion it was supported unanimously by all parties as being in the public interest and in the interest of the peace, order and good government of this country.

I do not find it. It does state that if there is any evasion the paper shall be denied the right to use the mails. Then we come to subdause 2; there is a form of penalty there, but applicable only to newspapers with paid circulation. I am thinking of newspapers such as are often circulated for which no payment is made. If those papers have no identification as to ownership they evade the provisions entirely. I have in mind newspapers that are circulated by the thousands, particularly at election time. No one knows where they come from or who publishes them; they may contain all kinds of scurrilous matter, and there is nothing in this bill to provide for them. I think if we are going to attempt to find out who publishes newspapers and is responsible for the disseminating of certain kinds of information, the bill should cover all classes of newspapers. As it is now the bill is not wide enough to take care of a situation which is the cause of a great deal of annoyance and worse. I have seen in the publications I refer to untruthful and lying statements, with no indication of the source or the name of the printer of the paper or of who was responsible for its publication. If it is at all possible, with the consent of the

Supply-Railways and Canals
mover of the bill I should like this clause to stand so that the point I have raised might be looked into. Perhaps the clause could be made wider so that it would include all classes of newspapers having circulation in the Dominion of Canada.

This bill is in exactly
the same form as the bill I have introduced four or five times previously; there has not been a word changed. Previously this bill passed the house unanimously and it had the support of farmers' newspapers as well as most other newspapers throughout this country.
Mr. HEAPS; What the hon. member says may be perfectly true, but it does not answer the question I have just raised or the definite statement I made as to incidents which have occurred in this country during the past five or six years. If the hon. member who has introduced this bill would be good enough to let the matter stand I should be glad to take up with him the clause about which I am complaining now and to give him information which perhaps will convince him of the desirability of making the scope of the bill a little wider, because from what I can see of it I believe it could be evaded very easily, so that it might not bring the benefit the hon. member hopes. Surely the whole
thing depends on whether or not the post office department decides to recognize any alleged publication as a newspaper within the meaning of the act. If that is so the objection of the hon. member for North Winnipeg is gone. On the other hand if it does not, then no person can say that the importance of a recognized newspaper attaches to it. That is all that it amounts to.

As I have already said,
I agree with the principle of the bill, but I strongly object to paragraph 4, which reads:
The Postmaster General may make such regulations as are required to carry out the provisions of this act.
I do not believe that power should be vested in one minister. If the hon. member for East Toronto is willing tc dispense with that paragraph I will support the bill.

May I say to the hon.
gentleman and to the hon. member for North Winnipeg that this bill was before this house in 1919, and the point raised to-night was
raised at that time. The question was asked then whether a bill of this kind did not interfere with the property and civil rights of the provinces, and we obtained the opinion of the Department of Justice, which was that it does not in any way infringe on the jurisdiction of the provinces in regard to property and civil rights. Under section 91 of the British North America Act the regulation of post offices is exclusively a matter for the federal government. This bill deals only with regulation of postal matters in regard to certain publications that have obtained franchises from this parliament in the way of second class rates; it provides that they must conform to this bill. I have no objection to a penalty, but a penalty is included in the bill, if hon. gentlemen will note it. These publications which do not comply with the terms of the bill are to be denied the use of the mails, and I think that penalty is sufficient.
What connection has subclause 2 with the Post Office Act? It has no connection at all; this is a separate matter.

I read the letter from
the Postmaster General of the United States with regard to penalties. This is simply a regulation of the Post Office Department.

But subclause 2 has no reference whatever to the post office; it simply says that if you do not indicate the material for the publication of which money has been paid you are liable to a fine of not less than $50 and not more than $500. That does not come under the jurisdiction of the Post Office Department; it comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces in connection with property and civil rights.

I think this bill contains
all the regulations and penalties necessary to meet the situation.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to discuss the so-called Montreal agreement. I have little doubt that the Minister of Railways and Canals knows a great deal more about the

Supply-Railways and Canals
Montreal agreement than I do, but that agreement has been the cause of a great deal of dissatisfaction and heartache to a great many men engaged in the running trades by the Canadian National Railways. In many districts of the road these differences have been adjusted, but that is not by any means the case over the whole road. Now, sir, in order that members of the committee may have some little knowledge of this affair perhaps I might take a moment or two to explain it. This may necessitate a little reiteration but I shall endeavour to be as speedy as possible.
When the lines that now form the Canadian National system were consolidated and combined the management set about rehabilitating the road. It was found that the Canadian Northern, being considerably older than either the Grand Trunk Pacific or the National Transcontinental, was in much worse repair, and in order to put the roadbed in shape it was found necessary to start a great number of extra hauling crews. Some fifty engine crews were started on the Canadian Northern portion of the system at that time. Subsequently, when the various portions were consolidated and combined, and the road was put on a running basis, it was discovered that there was a ratio of four crews on the Canadian Northern portion of the road to one crew on any other portion of the road. Since a good deal of the freight and other business was routed over the newer portions, namely the Canadian government parts of the road, this led to considerable dissatisfaction on the part Of the engineers and firemen of the old Canadian Northern railway system. An agitation was set on foot which resulted in the matter being taken up by the grand lodges of engineers and firemen assembled at Cleveland, Ohio, and in committees being appointed, such committees to consist of the presidents and the eight vice-presidents of the respective brotherhoods. These men conferred and decided upon an equitable arrangement whereby they gave the Canadian Northern engine men a ratio of seven, as compared with two for the Grand Trunk Pacific and one for the Canadian government railways running east out of Trans-cona. The agreement was made, but apparently it was not very satisfactory, because, while it was to become effective in 1926, an injunction placed upon it prevented its becoming effective until 1928.

On the western lines. It
came into force on the eastern lines in 1926, and on the western in 1928.

I am interested in the
western lines, and I am speaking with regard to them. Even after it came into effect the

agreement was not satisfactory; in fact so far as the western lines are concerned it had never been satisfactory. May I explain at this point that the part of the system with which I am concerned and about which I complain consists of the old Canadian Northern terminus at Fort Rouge in the city of Winnipeg, and the Canadian government terminus at the town of Transcona, six miles east of Winnipeg. The arrangement was that the crews which had run out of Transcona should go to Fort Rouge and take out trains, and on the other hand that the crews of the Canadian Northern lines running out of Fort Rouge should likewise be in a position to go to Transcona and take out trains. As I stated previously the ratio was to stand at seven crews for the Canadian Northern portion, two crews for the Grand Trunk Pacific and one for the National Transcontinental. Singular as it may seem, the first men to complain, so far as this portion of the road is concerned, were the old Canadian Northern men, because after the arrangement was put into effect crews went from Transcona to Fort Rouge to take out passenger trains, and a very active protest was set on foot by the engineers of the Canadian Northern portion of the lines which was the cause of bringing into force an agreement known as the Montreal agreement, and which was engineered by a former Minister of Labour, the Hon. Peter Heenan. By this subsequent arrangement it was decided that engineers and firemen might not leave their own terminals to take out first and second class trains, namely passenger and mixed trains, so that the small ratio of men on the Canadian government railways were robbed of about the on'y consolation they had. The result of it all is that at the present time in Transcona there are about thirty engineers and about twice as many firemen who practically never get a run, and who see men who began working many years later running regularly from day to day. Obviously this is an unfair and prejudicial state of affairs.
In complaining about the matter to me these men set forth several points. They claim that the agreement was entirely unfair in every sense for the reasons-
First, that the test was made in the month of September, 1920, when the road was abnormally busy carrying grain.
Second, owing to the comparatively small size of engines on the Canadian Northern portion and the fact that one engine of standard size such as was then operating on the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian government line was hauling three times the tonnage of the former, there were therefore

Supply-Railways and Canals
three times the number of engine crews engaged on the Canadian Northern as would be required to haul the same tonnage on the other lines.
Third, at the time the test was made some fifty extra crews had been taken on the Canadian Northern portion for the purpose of improving and balancing the road bed.
Fourth, owing to a trestle bridge at Brere-ton, eighty miles east of Winnipeg on the Canadian government line, being washed out, all freight east had to be routed by the Canadian Northern railway out of Winnipeg, thus greatly augmenting business on that portion of the system and leaving traffic practically at a standstill on the Canadian government lines.
Fifth, the most important point is that owing to the fact that the small number of Canadian government men in the order formed a minority they were overwhelmingly outvoted when the matter was brought up in the grand lodge at Cleveland.
Sixth, all efforts to obtain redress either through labour organizations, through the management or by any means whatsoever have failed, and left them helpless.
Seventh, -and this is rather important-
Would the hon. member permit a question? I ask only for information. Does he know what percentage of the men claim they have been unjustly treated? I must confess I have no information on the point.
I do not know the percentage, but I know the number in the town of Transcona, which is in my constituency. It involves thirty engineers and about twice as many firemen.
Out of a total of how many?

Well, they represent practically all of the old Canadian government lines engineers, on the lines running east from Transcona. These men are out of work They have been thrown off their lines, and outsiders have come in and taken their work with the result that they have nothing to do.
The seventh point, and one worthy of consideration, is that the Canadian Northern men were given seniority or priority from the time they started wiping in the shops, and the men on the Grand Trunk Pacific and on the Canadian government lines were given seniority only from the date of their first run on an engine on the road. Sometimes this made a very considerable difference. Then, there is a minor consideration which,
however, means a good deal to the men on the road. Former Canadian Northern men living in Winnipeg and either leaving or arriving at Transcona during the night have a big, comfortable bunkhouse at their disposal, in which they may spend that portion of the night remaining to them either before departure or after arrival. On the other hand the Transcona men, former employees of the Canadian government railways, must travel six miles through to Fort Rouge in order to take their trains, or go in to Winnipeg the evening before and engage a room in the hotel or a boarding house in order to avoid the trip into the city during the night. Likewise the men who arrive over the Canadian Northern system at night are exposed to the necessity of taking a taxicab and driving home through the night or spending the night at a hotel, either of which means considerable expense. Someone may ask: Why don't they move? Well the difficulty is that they originally belonged to Transcona, and they still belong to Transcona. Many of them have their homes there, and that is where their living should be. They are exposed to the necessity of making a trip during the night into the city of Winnipeg in order to get a run on the road at all. It seems to me like a very unfair piece of business, and the men have without doubt I imagine indicated that in their complaint to the Minister of Railways, who probably has told them that it is no affair of his, that it is a matter for the management and the men. But when the men appeal to the management of the road the management tell them:	We have
nothing to do with it because we made an arrangement with your organization and we are quite helpless in the matter. Finally, when the men complain to their organization they are in a minority there, and are outvoted. Obviously it is unfair to these men at Transcona, and I presume that others on other parts of the road, have seen men who started ten or fifteen years later than themselves supplanting on their runs and taking their living out of their mouths.
What possibly can be done for them? It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the minister might with reason indicate to the management of the road that he considers this a decided unfairness, and he might ask the management to confer with the representatives of the labour organizations. The minister could point out to the management this obvious unfairness that was obtaining on the road and ask them to try to correct this situation and give these men a proper show. The fair thing would be to give all the men on the road

piority rights from the time they took their first trip on the road, and if these men had priority rights from the date of their first trip on the road I think that they would be satisfied.
The Fort Rouge men going to Transcona have a comfortable bunkhouse in which to spend the night. This may seem a small matter to bring up in the House of Commons, but let me say that it means a good deal to the men who have to make a trip through the night to get from Transcona to Winnipeg, If the management could provide a similar bunkhouse in Fort Rouge for the men who have to go into the city I think their grievances would be fairly well met and that they would be fairly satisfied. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, this matter ought to receive the consideration of the minister.

' I have listened attentively and with a good deal of interest to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Howden) has said, and I have no doubt he has made a perfectly fair and sincere statement of the whole situation. He is quite right in saying that the matter has been brought to my attention by other groups. I doubt, however, if the group to which he refers has brought it to my attention, although they may have done so in the five years I have been minister, but if they did I do not remember it. Undoubtedly it has been brought to my attention by certain of the groups. I remember particularly that some groups on the eastern lines in the extreme Atlantic region brought to my attention injustices which they claimed had' been imposed on them through the Montreal agreement.
Perhaps a very brief review of the Montreal agreement might be useful to the members of the committee, particularly those who were not here when the hon. gentleman started speaking before the dinner recess. According to my information, the Montreal agreement was not put into effect until December 1, 1926, on the eastern lines-the Atlantic region Central region and the Grand Trunk Western, and it was put into effect on the western lines just two years later.

It was held up by an
injunction on behalf of the men in the west.

After the injunction, or
rather after a board of conciliation had sat, the agreement came into effect on the western lines on May 1, 1928. The need for an agreement arose out of the consolidation of the various lines, as the hon. gentleman has stated, into the Canadian National group. The old Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk

Pacific, the National Transcontinental, the Intercolonial and so forth were taken over between 1918 and 1920 and consolidated into the national system, and, just as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, various groups representing men on the old roads, which were independently operated in the first place, demanded their seniority rights. As traffic was shifted from one portion of the railway to another, where it could be more economically handled, certain groups of men were thrown out of their positions. For example, it might have been found that traffic coming from Winnipeg to Fort William over one route before the amalgamation could be handled more economically after the amalgamation by bringing it over another route, and consequently the group from which the traffic was taken found themselves without their accustomed runs. There was so much trouble raised by the men themselves with the management, and rightly so, that the management in a sense said to them: For heaven's sake get together and settle your seniority rights. After a period of years the men got together, and finally on the dates I mentioned, in 1926 for the Atlantic. Central, and Grand Trunk Western lines, and in 1928 for the western region they came to these agreements so far as the firemen and engineers are concerned. After a conciliation board under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act had sat, the western region finally came under the agreement on May 1, 1928. It was the men themselves and their organizations which arranged the Montreal agreement. Undoubtedly some injustices have been done, and I have no doubt that the case as cited by my hon. friend has been stated correctly. I know from complaints that I have received from other sections that other injustices have also been done. But as the hon. gentleman pointed out in his closing remarks, I have no power in the matter. It was arranged first of all by the men themselves through their various organizations, and then they submitted it to the management, and the management accepted it as the best arrangement which could be come to.
The management now .takes the attitude when I bring these cases before them-I have done so before, and I shall gladly draw their attention to the statements and suggestions of my hon. friend-that while undoubtedly some injustices have been done this is an arrangement which is for the greatest good of the greatest number, and that if they attempt to interfere with it, it would bring about such a chaotic condition that there would be no satisfaction whatever; in other

words, while there are a few dissatisfied now, if they changed the arrangement ail w-ould be dissatisfied and chaos would result.
LTnder these circumstances I really do not know what can be done. My hon. friend's final suggestion might be a very simple solution or a part solution of the situation locally, and I think it is well worthy of consideration. I refer to the proposal he made as to a bunk-house. But that would solve the difficulty only as far as his section is concerned, and then perhaps only partly, because I assume the men who feel dissatisfied over losing their positions will still be dissatisfied to a certain extent. The only thing I can do, and I shall do it gladly, is to bring my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the management and ask them to give them whatever consideration they can. It is entirely a matter in the control of the men themselves and their organizations, and the management. I shall gladly bring the remarks of my hon. friend to the attention of the management for whatever consideration they can give them.

I want to thank the minister for his kind reception of my statement of the situation and for his consideration. I understand that their differences have been adjusted somehow or other and that Transcona is about the only sore spot left, and obviously the simple thing to do would be to give every man. his seniority from the time be made his first run on the road. As it is now, only some men are given seniority from the time they made their first run, other men being given seniority from the time they went into the shops ^ to wipe. They get the advantage of the time they spent wiping, and they are benefited to this extent in comparison with the other men.

The statement of the hon. gentleman is a repetition of what he said before and it does sound unjust, but the question of seniority among the men is not for the management; it rests entirely with the men themselves.
I quite agree with the minister in that regard.

It is a matter which is entirely in the hands of the men's organizations and the only people who can interfere with it are the men themselves. However, I shall he glad to bring the matter to the attention of the management-the only body with whom I have communication.-and ask them to give it every consideration, to see whether they can put it to .the men's organizations in such a wiay as to be of assistance.

I think the minister is absolutely sound. I hold no brief for the railway organizations; they are capable of speaking for themselves. But I think it is fair to say that whatever conditions are enjoyed by them, and they compare favourably with the conditions enjoyed by railway men in any other country, have been brought about by the organizations themselves through the instrumentality of the men to whom the hon. member has referred. What is the position of the government in this matter? There already exists in the country the proper machinery whereby the majority vote of these organizations prevails. If my hon. friend's contention is sound, then we on this side of the house should be the government and those on the government side should be sitting to the left of the Speaker. I think it would be a dangerous precedent for the government of the country to interfere unnecessarily while the proper machinery exists-the conciliation boards and so on-to rectify the grievances from which the men suffer or think they suffer. It places the government in the position of the boss, telling the men's organizations what they should do after they have decided on a certain policy according to sound democratic principles. I think the best thing these men can do is to get back into their organization and try to influence its policy; otherwise it would be a case of the tail wagging the dog. There may be some injustices-and I have had some experience with conciliation boards; I know something about seniority, and I know that men fight harder for seniority than for working conditions and wages. That exists in every line where the strict policy of seniority prevails. But to ask even the employers to dictate to the organizations what they shall do, when one considers the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, is to propose something which in my opinion is beyond the ken of the government, of the management and of the members of this House of Commons.
In other words, the hon. member for East Hamilton declares that the policy of the government has been right from start to finish.
Absence of policy.

I was not suggesting that the government should interfere; I was suggesting to the minister that the government might indicate to the management of the road the desirability of having this matter

reviewed and adjusted if possible. The hon. member for Hamilton spoke of some men I kinking that they were unfairly used.
The hon. gentleman means East Hamilton; I am the member for Hamilton.

Hamilton anyway. Well,
I have here a slip indicating that one It. H. Bailey hired with the Canadian Government Railways in 1915, and he is now behind a man hired after 1920. Obviously he is unfairly treated. Another man, Huston by name, hired originally in 1911. He w7ent overseas and came back and is now firing for a man who must have been fifteen years of age when he commenced railroading in order to be this other man's senior. There can be little doubt that in these two instances these men are discriminated against. As regards having the order adjust these matters, every time the question has been brought to a vote in the order the men in the majority outvote the men in the minority, and the men in the minority take what they can get, which is nothing. That is the way it works out in the order.

The organizations have the sole right to handle the seniority problems of their particular railways; the management have never interfered and do not pretend to interfere. The Minister of Railways, I think, gave about as clear an explanation as it is possible for anyone to give, with this exception. They have had what are known as general seniority promotions, over quite a large territory, and when the amalgamation took place a large number of men voluntarily moved from one part of the district to another. The hon. member for St. Boniface is no doubt absolutely correct in stating that a number of men in Transcona have been done an injustice; but while these particular men on that particular railway may have been done an injustice, nevertheless, taking it as a whole, it was the very best program that the representatives of the men could work out to suit the country as a whole. And as the minister has pointed out, it would upset conditions terribly if an attempt were made to adjust the matter at this late date. The man representing the Canadian Northern at that time has received promotion from his organization; so evidently, as a whole, they must have been satisfied with the work he did for the men.

In 1926 and 1928 I sent a strong protest to Sir Henry Thornton with regard to the universal promotion scheme. It comes from the Montreal agreement. Now,
[ Mr. Howden.]
it works in a very strange way. At a division point some employees who have been working for twenty years are set back and other men who have been working only ten years have still an opportunity to work. There is discrimination there, and I bring it to the attention of the minister. No one intends to interfere with the high policy of the management, but on the other hand it is only fair to bring these instances to the attention of the government in order that they may be transmitted to the management, and the management can see whether there is some way of reaching a compromise with the men. I agree with my hon. friend from East Hamilton; the matter should be settled by mutual agreement between the management and the men. The Montreal agreement should be amended by mutual consent, just in the same way as it was made, but in order to bring that about, it must be discussed and the matter should be brought to the attention of the management.
I shall be glad if the minister will see that that is done.
I will bring the whole discussion to the attention of the management.
I thank the minister.

This may not be the proper item, but may I once again draw the attention of the minister to what is known as the Bulwark Easterly line in Alberta on which some twenty-five miles of grading has been done for some years. The people in that vicinity had great hopes that the line would be completed. Needless to say, being quite a long way from the railway, they have been greatly handicapped in getting their grain and other produce to market, and they have been waiting very patiently in the hope that something will be done. Is there any prospect that the rails may be put on this grade as part of the relief work that it is anticipated the government will bring before the house this session?

The line to which the hon. member refers is in exactly the same position as most of the other branch lines which have been spoken of and drawn to my attention at various times in the last three or four years. The question is one of the management recommending the continuation of some of these lines, and because of the financial condition of the railways, the management has not seen fit to recommend the continuation of any of them so far as I know. I may suggest to the hon. member as I did to the hon. member for North Battleford, that we did have yesterday and we shall probably have again on Tuesday.

Wednesday and Thursday of next week the managing officers of the Canadian National Railways before the select standing committee on railways and shipping, and since the hon. gentleman is very much interested in the matter, he might have a chat with Mr. Fullerton and Mr. Hungerford in regard to this line and just see if he can influence them, because the suggestion and recommendation have in the final result to come from them. If they take the attitude that this line rather than some others requires attention, he may rest assured that the government will do everything it can to carry out the recommendation of the railways. Their recommendations are generally speaking carried out. When those officials are here again for two or three days next week, the hon. member might interview them in regard to the matter. I will repeat to him what I said to the hon. member for North Battleford: I would have no objection and I am sure the other members of the committee would have none to his coming into the committee and asking the question directly, because the officials are in a better position than I am to decide the matter.

I had intended to go to the railway committee and ask permission, but I happen to be a member of the banking and' commerce committee and it has been sitting at the same time. If I have an opportunity next week, I shall take advantage of the offer made by the minister. I am quite sure the people for whom I am speaking do not wish any favours, but they do want not to be overlooked. If these lines which are half finished are going to be completed, they think they should be given the same treatment as the others.

May I say a word further without seeking in any way to delay my own estimates? I have every sympathy for all those different groups that have branch lines partly constructed or that have been promised branch lines, but as the hon. member knows,; the question has been one of the finances of the railways. I hope in the very near future the railways will feel able to recommend and the government will feel able to support the recommendation for the further construction1 of these branch lines. I hope my hon. friend will come before the committee and submit his case to the management of the railways.
I will.

No tolls whatever. But

Yes. .

Do we receive reciprocal
privileges from other countries?

There are charges on the
Panama canal, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) pointed out. As to the Manchester canal my engineer is not sure; as to the Kiel canal, I imagine they have tolls. But we are in this rather difficult position, that there are treaty arrangements with many different countries, and aside from them the big difficulty is the United States. For example at Sault Ste. Marie the United States has the better canal and our ships largely use the American canal in preference to our own. It is true that down here the Welland is the big canal; in fact the United States have none at that point. But it was
found prior to 1903 or 1904, when tolls were abandoned that tolls diverted the traffic from the Canadian canals to Buffalo and down through the Erie canal to New York. In other words if we put tolls on in the east the Americans who have the best canal in the upper lakes can retaliate, as they did once, by putting on tolls in respect of shipping using their Sault Ste. Marie canal. Those might balance and not matter much, but when we come to the St. Lawrence canals, grain, which in the absence of tolls goes down the St. Lawrence and out by Canadian ports would be diverted at Buffalo and exported through American ports. For these reasons it was decided a third of a century ago that it was better not to charge canal tolls, in order to hold the grain and other traffic. I remember looking into the matter before the war and finding that at least one-third of our Canadian grain went to New York. I have not the figures now; I think a less proportion goes that way now. Of course in the meantime the port of Vancouver has taken a great deal of traffic that used to go east, much to the surprise of some people-

They used to laugh at the
idea.

They did not so much laugh, but they were afraid that the wheat could not go south through Panama without heating. I remember reading many articles to that effect. But as a matter of fact about half goes that way now. My engineer shows me that for 1933 the amount of Canadian wheat going down the St. Lawrence and out by Canadian ports was 88,000,000 bushels and via Buffalo and New York 35,000,000. That is about the same proportion as before the war; a little more than one-third went via Buffalo in 1933. I have no later figures. In 1932 the figures were almost exactly the same. In 1931 it was about fifty fifty; half went each way. That is Canadian wheat, of course, and it must be remembered that a certain amount of United States wheat goes out by Montreal, which offsets some of our wheat that goes the other way.

I am trying to get at the
economics of the whole thing at the moment. The Welland canal costs the country from $6,000,000 to $7,000,000 a year, and I am just wondering whether from an economic standpoint and from the standpoint of the amount of benefit we receive from it the Welland canal is worth it.

A question was asked in this house about stevedoring charges, and the minister I think quite properly replied that the government had very little to do with it, that the shipping companies contracted with certain stevedoring contractors who carried on the work. That is quite true, but I am not going to go quite as far as the minister and say that the government have no responsibility in the matter because I think it is a responsibility upon this government to see that the people using that route get a square deal and get the lowest possible rates for stevedoring, dock and harbour charges that it is possible to give them. I am going to give a comparative statement of the stevedoring charges in Churchill and Montreal in support of my statement that we are not getting a square deal at Churchill from the stevedores.
At Churchill, for 270,000 bushels shipped,
the stevedoring charge is 84 a thousand bushels, or 81,080; bagging grain. 5,000 at 9 cents, 8450, or a total of 81,530, less ten per cent. I believe the discount of ten per cent is universal. The charges at Montreal are

I do not say that the season should be advanced a month or six weeks at a time, but this year it might have been moved up to the first of August and, in my opinion, it could with safety be moved to the 15th of July. A boat cannot get into trouble either in the
straits or in the bay even if it sights an iceberg, because at that time of the year there is daylight twenty-four hours of the day, and there are no shoals or reefs.
