It is not unreasonable, from the reports that come from that boat, to ask that the season be extended a little. No injustice is being done by the government, and neither the shipping committee nor the government can change ice conditions and allow ships to come in. I did not suggest

But it does not matter if a boat does get into the ice; nothing can happen to her, because she has only to lie there until the wind blows the ice away. I appreciate what the department have done and are doing, and I thank them for it. I feel at Churchill they have one of the finest staffs of men that 
I have come into contact with in my life so far as administration work is concerned. They cheerfully do everything they can for everybody who goes in there and are very highly spoken of by all the captains and others who enter that port. I want to thank the officials for what they are doing at Churchill and for the interest they are showing in the route; I refer especially to the officials at the port. I think the time has arrived, now that construction work has been completed, that the government should interest themselves in trying to get some more business for that route. The Department of Railways and Canals, whether it operates directly or through the Canadian National Railways who are acting as its agents, is selling transportation; it is also selling port facilities and elevator storage and facilities. If you want to sell goods these days, you must advertise. I stated before in the house that there was one handicap in securing business for that route, although the Saskatchewan wheat pool I believe made good use of it last year and saved themselves something like two and one-half cents a bushel by doing so, even at the high insurance rates and excessive cost of shipping. I believe they intend to make greater use of that route this year. There were also shipped out of Churchill five hundred head of cattle, and the man who shipped them informed me that they netted the producer $35 a head, whereas he could not have got more than $12 a head had he shipped them to Winnipeg or Prince Albert stockyard. This would mean something to the sections of western Canada that this road can economically serve.
An hon. member asked the minister whether he could give him any idea of the prospects for next year. As I said, they made a saving of about two and one-half cents a bushel, which will be increased by almost a cent by the reduction in insurance rates in the coming season. The time has now arrived for some cooperation between the Hudson Bay Railway and the port of Churchill, and the Canadian National Railway officials and employees.

Before my hon. friend

Some steps should be taken to create a colonization department in connection with that route. There are thousands of acres of first class agricultural land along that road. Many people have had to leave the dry belts in the south and to go north looking for some new spots in which to start over again. I do not know of any better place that men with that pioneering spirit could go to than up along the Hudson Bay railway. You can grow there almost anything you can grow anywhere else in Canada except fruits, and there are wild fruits there. You can grow grain and roots equal in quality and yield to that raised in any other part of the country; that is amply demonstrated at anv point where the train stops. The settlers going in there would have an opportunity which they would not have in some of the other northern sections and into which they are going now, due to the fact that the lakes along that road are teeming with fish. There are also plenty of game and fur bearing animals and they could pick up a little bit of fur in the winter which would help them at the time they needed money most. When this item
was up for discussion last year, and the question of marine insurance came up, the minister admitted that, notwithstanding the reductions given, the rates on the Hudson Bay route were still four or five times as high as on the St. Lawrence route. The acting Prime Minister a week or so ago, when announcing a twenty-five per cent reduction, did not say exactly how it was to be figured, but I understand it still leaves the rate three or four times as high by the Hudson Bay route as by the St. Lawrence. It seeems to me that the greatest handicap to this port is not icebergs or shoals or anything of that kind, but the abnormally high marine insurance rate. I have never blamed the minister for it very much; I suppose it is one of the handicaps that all new routes have to contend with. It has been the story of navigation all the world over from time immemorial, any new ocean, rail or caravan route has that great handicap to fight. But it seems to me that if we really mean to get the fullest use from this investment something else will have to be done to get over the uncertainty regarding the alleged dangers of the route. The insurance men in London are not going to worry about it. It is a small matter, to them; they are not going to take any chances but will let time demonstrate what the risks are. Meantime some of us are getting past middle life and would like to see more benefit being obtained and more use made of this port, after having spent part of a lifetime getting it. Did it ever occur to the minister that something more might be done? This is a day of talk about state ownership and reforms of one

kind and1 another; would it not constitute a great reform for the government to step in and shorten this period of uncertainty by assuming some share of the obligation of experimentation? Other ports might object, you may say. Well, I recall quite well that the Vancouver outlet for grain was assisted by the building of a second railway with very low grades, also by very low rates, the Crowsnest rates by the Yellowhead pass route, with the result that trade began to flow via the Pacific route, but not until those advantages were given it. Now we have this other route by Hudson bay, and the Crowsnest rates have been applied there. But it occurs to me that the- government might do worse than establish a marine insurance branch in the Department of Marine and Fisheries to provide marine insurance for all Canadian ports, at cost plus whatever reserve is necessary to take care of contingencies. That would be a great advantage to the St. Lawrence route also, as it would not then have the disadvantage of a higher rate than shipments via American Atlantic ports. That seems to me worth considering, and it would be fair to all ports. We speak about restrictions and handicaps on our ports, and there are grave restrictions on the use of our ports, without going into it in detail. Anything that would facilitate the greater use of our ports would be of advantage to our railways and to everyone concerned, particularly as there is little or no marine insurance written in this country. I commend Ihe idea to the minister. In spite of the fact that he represents a rival port I think he has not done too badly-I will give him that commendation; but he is not galloping in the direction of helping Hudson bay. For not being as bad as he might have been I give him the credit that is coming to him. I would not be making this suggestion now if I did not think he would give it at least fair consideration. It would be in the interests of Canada to establish marine insurance for all our ports, put them all on an equal footing and see what can be done in regard to attracting a greater volume of trade to our shores, to all our ports and especially Hudson bay. The Atlantic ports, Saint John and Halifax, have the advantage of proximity, the short haul across the Atlantic, and being open all the year-I understand in some years Saint John is not open the whole year, but Halifax is.

If I may be permitted to correct my hon. friend, Saint John is open all the year round.

Well, I am glad to be corrected. I was merely pointing out that they are not in need of as much sympathy as either Hudson bay or the St. Lawrence route, and neither is Vancouver nor other Pacific ports. Anything that tends to drive away traffic is a handicap to a port. A government that professes to be introducing reforms would accomplish a real reform by taking such an advanced step. I am of the opinion that we are in the grip of a huge insurance combine. Perhaps that is not the way to put it, but we are in the hands of one company, and it is situated overseas. It is under those circumstances, when there is a real cinch obtained on any business, that governments are justified in intervening. I am not usually an advocate of governments rushing into business, except when there is some abuse to correct, but it looks to me as if we are in the hands of practically one marine insurance company on the other side of the Atlantic. Here is the finest chance in the world for a real reform with the least disturbance of established business that you could conceive of; and anyway, why not give our ports the advantage of the cheapest insurance rates consistent with meeting the cost? I would like the minister to express his views on this.
No doubt the hon. gentleman is quite sincere in his suggestion, even though he did rather damn me with faint praise-
I think I was pretty fair.

Oh, yes, the hon. gentleman and I have been very fair to each other for a long time now. But I doubt if the government of Canada would be justified, whether this government or any other, in going into the insurance business in any port. As I pointed out a few moments ago, according to last year's returns we were down $208,000 in round figures in operation alone, and that of course allows nothing for interest on the rather huge investment. As my hon. friend says, the matter of insurance is under the control of the imperial shipping committee, but I doubt if they would be particularly interested in interfering in any way -with the port of Churchill. Undoubtedly the rates at Churchill will gradually improve as the route proves itself, so to speak. The unfortunate accident that happened two or three years ago, the sinking of the Bright Fan, no doubt threw back some considerable distance the lowering of the insurance rates at that port. It was one of those unfortunate
accidents that I do not think should be blamed on the port, but as I understand it the insurance companies figure out their rates on an actuarial basis, and the loss that had to be paid in connection with the Bright Fan no doubt wiped out whatever profits might accrue in connection with Churchill for quite a time. Consequently as time goes on the insurance rates will go down, and I believe they will go down fairly rapidly because I agree with much that was said by my hon. friend from Nelson in regard to Churchill. I have heard the captains of some steamships make very complimentary remarks about the route and the ease with which they can navigate it; I heard those remarks on two occasions when I was there, and I think in the near future, as traffic increases, there will* be no difficulty about the rates coming down. The government are acting very energetically on that question, just as I am sure my hon. friends would continue to act if by any misfortune they should be returned to power after the next election. I doubt very much, however, if any government would be justified in going into the insurance business; I rather feel that the government of Canada is in a sufficient number of businesses already. My hon. friend mentioned the chief objection himself when he pointed out that you could hardly pick out one port and more or less root for it, if I may use a street expression. My hon. friend from .Nelson, who deserves a great deal of credit for the energetic way in which he has boosted that route and that section of the country, brought up another question. He thought the government should go out and, in a sense, solicit traffic for the Hudson Bay route. This generation will pass on without knowing much of the benefits of that short route. Some day, by some fortune, if we have a great amount of traffic such as we have had in other years, when the peak load will require every conceivable outlet in the fall of the year, probably Churchill will be used more, but I do not think we should wait for that accident to happen.
